name: NRF52840-QIAA-R
title: nRF52840 multiprotocol Bluetooth 5, IEEE 802.15.4 and 2.4 GHz SoC, Arm Cortex-M4F 64 MHz, 1 MB flash, 256 kB RAM, USB
summary: A 2.4 GHz system-on-chip for Bluetooth 5 (including 2 Mbps and long range), IEEE 802.15.4 and proprietary radios, built round a 64 MHz Arm Cortex-M4 with FPU, 1 MB of flash and 256 kB of RAM. It runs from 1.7 V to 3.6 V on VDD or 2.5 V to 5.5 V on VDDH through on-chip LDO and DC/DC regulators, and carries full-speed USB, QSPI, an NFC-A tag, a CryptoCell 310 security block, a 12-bit ADC and 48 GPIOs. The nRF52840-QIAA is the 7 x 7 mm aQFN73 version; the part is also offered as QFN48 (QFAA) and WLCSP (CKAA).
key_figures: VDD 1.7 V to 3.6 V; VDDH 2.5 V to 5.5 V; VBUS 4.35 V to 5.5 V
-95 dBm at 1 Mbps BLE; -103 dBm at 125 kbps
4.8 mA TX at 0 dBm, 4.6 mA RX (peak)
0.4 µA System OFF; 1.5 µA System ON with RTC wake, at 3 V
USB 2.0 full speed, QSPI, SPI, I2C, UART, I2S, PDM, NFC-A
aQFN73 7 x 7 mm (QIAA); also QFN48 and WLCSP

circuits.title: aQFN73 configuration 1: USB supply on VDDH, LDO regulators
circuits.description: Reference circuit for the nRF52840-QIAA. USB-powered: VBUS reaches VDDH and the VBUS pin through the optional 2.2 Ω resistor R1, with C19 on that node. The internal regulator makes VDD_nRF, which also leaves the circuit as VEXT. C20 decouples DECUSB. Both DC/DC stages are off, so DCC and DCCH are left open. The 32 MHz crystal X1 sits across XC1/XC2 with C1 and C2 to ground; the optional 32.768 kHz crystal X2 sits across XL1/XL2 with C17 and C18. C5 decouples DEC1, C11 DEC3 and C9 DEC5 (C9 only on build codes Dxx and earlier); DEC2 has a not-mounted place C13. DEC4 and DEC6 are joined and carry C15, with a not-mounted place C10. VDD_nRF reaches every VDD pin with C6, C14, C12, C7 and C8 beside them. The antenna pin feeds a pi match: C3 to ground, L1 in series, then C4 to ground, into a 50 Ω antenna; C22 is an unmounted place. C3 returns to ground through the VSS_PA pin. SWDIO and SWDCLK are brought out for debug; no other part connects to the GPIOs.

operation.text: 2.4 GHz transceiver for Bluetooth 5, IEEE 802.15.4-2006 and proprietary links, air-compatible with the nRF52, nRF51, nRF24L and nRF24AP Series. Data rates: Bluetooth 5 at 2 Mbps, 1 Mbps, 500 kbps and 125 kbps; 802.15.4 at 250 kbps; proprietary at 2 Mbps and 1 Mbps. Sensitivity is -95 dBm at 1 Mbps Bluetooth LE and -103 dBm at 125 kbps (long range). Output power runs from -20 to +8 dBm in 4 dB steps. Peak current is 4.8 mA transmitting at 0 dBm and 4.6 mA receiving. RSSI resolves 1 dB. The antenna output is single-ended with the balun on chip, and a 128-bit AES ECB/CCM/AAR co-processor encrypts packets on the fly.
Arm Cortex-M4 with floating-point unit at 64 MHz: 212 EEMBC CoreMark running from flash, at 52 µA/MHz. Debug is serial wire (SWD) with the DWT, ETM and ITM watchpoint and trace units.

Arm TrustZone CryptoCell 310 subsystem: random number generator meeting NIST SP800-90A and SP800-90B; AES-128 in ECB, CBC, CMAC/CBC-MAC, CTR and CCM/CCM*; ChaCha20/Poly1305 AEAD with 128- and 256-bit keys; SHA-1 and SHA-2 up to 256 bits; HMAC; RSA keys up to 2048 bits; SRP up to 3072 bits; elliptic-curve support for the common curves including P-256 (secp256r1) and Ed25519/Curve25519; application key management by a derived-key model. For secure boot: flash access control list (ACL), root of trust, debug control and configuration, access port protection (CTRL-AP). Secure erase.

Supply range 1.7 V to 5.5 V. On-chip DC/DC and LDO regulators drop to low-current modes on their own, and a regulated 1.8 V to 3.3 V supply is available for outside parts. Peripheral power is managed automatically and a 64 MHz internal oscillator gives a fast wake-up. At 3 V: 0.4 µA in System OFF with no RAM retained; 1.5 µA in System ON with no RAM retained and wake on RTC.

1 MB flash and 256 kB RAM. Full-speed (12 Mbps) USB 2.0 controller, 32 MHz QSPI, 32 MHz high-speed SPI, type 2 NFC-A tag with wake-on-field and touch-to-pair, programmable peripheral interconnect (PPI), 48 GPIO pins and EasyDMA moving data between memory and peripherals. Ready for Nordic SoftDevices, including concurrent multiprotocol use.

12-bit 200 ksps ADC with 8 configurable channels and programmable gain; 64-level comparator; 15-level low-power comparator that can wake the chip from System OFF; temperature sensor. Four PWM units of four channels each with EasyDMA; I2S and PDM digital microphone interface; five 32-bit timers with counter mode; up to four SPI masters and three SPI slaves with EasyDMA; up to two I2C-compatible two-wire interfaces (master or slave); two UARTs with CTS/RTS and EasyDMA; quadrature decoder (QDEC); three real-time counters (RTC). Runs from a single crystal.
aQFN73 7 x 7 mm, QFN48 6 x 6 mm and WLCSP 3.544 x 3.607 mm.

Computer peripherals and I/O devices (mouse, keyboard, multi-touch trackpad); wearables (health and fitness sensors, wireless payment); IoT (smart home and industrial sensors and controllers); interactive entertainment (remote controls, gaming controllers).

Each peripheral has an upper-case name or abbreviation, such as TIMER, which is also its name in the CMSIS hardware abstraction layer. A peripheral that exists more than once is numbered from 0 (TIMER0, TIMER1 and so on), and that instance name is used in CMSIS too.

The Cortex-M4 (with NVIC, SysTick and ETM) and the EasyDMA masters of the peripherals share an AHB multilayer interconnect with RAM0 to RAM8, the GPIO block and the code memory behind an instruction cache; an AHB-to-APB bridge reaches the peripherals. Debug enters through the SW-DP with an AHB-AP and the CTRL-AP, and trace leaves through the TPIU. Instances: RTC0 to RTC2, TIMER0 to TIMER4, PWM0 to PWM3, SPIM0 to SPIM3, SPIS0 to SPIS2, TWIM0 and TWIM1, TWIS0 and TWIS1, UARTE0 and UARTE1, plus one each of RADIO, USBD, NFCT, QSPI, I2S, PDM, QDEC, SAADC, COMP, LPCOMP, GPIOTE, PPI, WDT, RNG, TEMP, ECB, CCM, AAR, CryptoCell, POWER, CLOCK, NVMC, FICR and UICR. Ports P0 (P0.0 to P0.31) and P1 (P1.0 to P1.15).

The core is an Arm Cortex-M4 with single-precision FPU, running the Thumb-2 mixed 16/32-bit instruction set. It has DSP instructions, single-cycle multiply-accumulate, a hardware divider and 8- and 16-bit SIMD. CMSIS is available for it, and interrupts at configurable priorities go through the NVIC with deterministic timing in thread mode and into and out of sleep. Code run from flash pays wait states; an instruction cache in the NVMC cuts them. SysTick is fitted and counts only while the CPU runs or the part is in debug interface mode. The CPU clock is 64 MHz.
An FPU exception such as overflow or underflow raises the FPU interrupt (peripheral ID 38, base 0x40026000). The interrupt line stays set until the matching exception bit in FPSCR is cleared.

There is 1024 kB of flash and 256 kB of RAM, usable for code and data. The CPU and the EasyDMA peripherals reach memory through the AHB multilayer interconnect, and the CPU reaches the peripherals through it too. One physical RAM appears twice: as Data RAM from 0x20000000 on the system bus and as Code RAM from 0x00800000 on ICODE/DCODE, so the application must split it so that code and data do not overlap.

RAM sits behind nine AHB slaves. Slaves RAM0 to RAM7 each carry two 4 kB sections; RAM8 carries six 32 kB sections. Every section has its own power and retention setting, separately for System ON and for System OFF, set in the POWER peripheral's RAM[n].POWER registers.
The CPU may read flash without limit, but writes and erases are counted and go through the NVMC. Flash is 256 pages of 4 kB, read over the ICODE and DCODE buses.

The non-volatile memory controller writes and erases the internal flash and the UICR. CONFIG.WEN selects write enable (Wen) or erase enable (Een). An NVMC operation started from the debugger needs the CPU halted first. While the NVMC writes or erases, a CPU fetching code from flash is stalled.

With writing enabled, whole 32-bit words go to word-aligned addresses; a byte or half-word access faults. A write can only clear erased bits (1 to 0); to change fewer than 32 bits, write the word with the untouched bits set to 1. Each word takes nWRITE writes at most between erases, and a write takes tWRITE. When READYNEXT reads 1 the next word may be written: it is buffered and goes in once the current write ends.

ERASEPAGE erases one 4 kB page to all ones in tERASEPAGE. UICR is written like flash, the new values act only after a reset, and it is erased with ERASEUICR (tERASEPAGE) or ERASEALL. ERASEALL clears all of flash and UICR in tERASEALL and leaves FICR alone.

To avoid long CPU stalls, a page erase can be cut into slices: ERASEPAGEPARTIAL runs an erase for the time set in ERASEPAGEPARTIALCFG; once the slices sum to tERASEPAGE the erase is complete, which counts as one erase cycle. It works on the code area only, not on UICR. Until the total reaches tERASEPAGE the contents of that flash page are undefined.

The I-cache on the ICODE bus answers a hit with no wait state; a miss costs the flash wait states (WFLASH). It can raise speed and lower current by cutting flash accesses, but draws some current itself, so the gain depends on the hit rate. Disabled, it draws nothing and keeps nothing. ICACHECNF turns on profiling: IHIT and IMISS count hits and misses and stop at full scale instead of wrapping. The cache holds 2048 bytes.
The factory information configuration registers at 0x10000000 hold chip-specific data and settings written at the factory; the user cannot erase them.

The user information configuration registers at 0x10001000 are non-volatile settings, written and erased through the NVMC like flash; erased, every word reads 0xFFFFFFFF. PSELRESET[0] and PSELRESET[1] must hold the same value for the nRESET pin mapping to take effect; if they differ, no GPIO acts as nRESET and the part starts regardless of the level on any GPIO. In High voltage mode the REGOUT0 setting may be no higher than VDDH less the REG0 dropout VVDDH-VDD.

EasyDMA is an AHB bus master built into some peripherals that reads and writes Data RAM directly; it cannot reach flash. A peripheral may have several channels, typically a reader and a writer, each set by a PTR (start address) and MAXCNT (largest transfer in bytes); after a transfer AMOUNT holds the number of bytes moved. MAXCNT must not exceed the buffer or the channel overruns it. PTR resets to no guaranteed address and must point into Data RAM before use: a pointer outside it may cause a HardFault or corrupt RAM. When several masters want the same RAM slave the bus congests, and depending on the peripheral it either stalls or loses data.

Channels with a LIST register can run in array-list mode: the buffers lie back to back in RAM, each MAXCNT bytes long, and the channel moves on to the next one in line; there is no pointer to the next item.

Every bus master connects to every slave through a matrix, and contention for one slave is settled by priority: the higher master goes first and lower ones stall until it finishes, though a lower master may use the slave while the higher one pauses. Masters of equal priority are mutually exclusive. Masters are the CPU and the EasyDMA peripherals; slaves are the RAM AHB slaves. Peripherals without a safe stall, such as RADIO, can lose data at low priority, so concurrent masters on one slave should be avoided or kept within the bus bandwidth.

Debug is non-intrusive over two-pin serial wire debug (SWDCLK, SWDIO). Fitted are a flash patch and breakpoint unit with two literal and six instruction comparators, a DWT with four comparators, ITM, ETM, and a TPIU giving ITM and ETM data as 4-bit parallel trace or SWO trace of ITM data. The DAP is a standard CoreSight SW-DP with the CPU's AHB-AP plus a Nordic control access port, CTRL-AP. SWDIO has an internal pull-up and SWDCLK an internal pull-down.

With protection on, the debugger cannot read or write CPU registers or any memory-mapped address. How it works depends on the build code. Build codes Dxx and earlier (hardware controlled): off by default; writing Enabled to UICR.APPROTECT and then any reset turns it on; a CTRL-AP ERASEALL, which erases flash, UICR and RAM, turns it off again. Build codes Fxx and later (hardware and software controlled): on by default; CTRL-AP ERASEALL opens it (check CTRL-AP.APPROTECTSTATUS and repeat if needed), and it stays open until a pin reset, power-on or brownout reset, a watchdog reset outside debug interface mode, or a wake from real System OFF. To keep it open, program UICR.APPROTECT to HwDisabled (0x5A) and have firmware write SwDisable (0x5A) to APPROTECT.DISABLE at 0x40000558 after every such reset. For more security, program UICR.APPROTECT to Enabled and let firmware write Force (0x0) into APPROTECT.FORCEPROTECT at 0x40000550, which holds protection on until the next reset of any kind.

The control access port stays usable when protection shuts the other access ports. It offers a soft reset (RESET, offset 0x000; 1 holds the device in reset), ERASEALL (0x004) with its status (ERASEALLSTATUS, 0x008), the protection status (APPROTECTSTATUS, 0x00C) and its IDR (0x0FC).

A debugger must first ask for power through CxxxPWRUPREQ in the SWJ-DP before it can use AHB-AP or CTRL-AP. That request wakes the part from System OFF and sets the DIF flag in RESETREAS. The part stays in debug interface mode for as long as power is requested, and some peripherals act differently there. Current is higher in this mode, so the debugger should release the request when the session ends.
With breakpoints in thread mode or in low-priority interrupts, higher-priority interrupts still run to completion in real time, so stepping through code does not break time-critical handlers.

ETM and ITM trace leave through the TPIU, either 4-bit parallel (TRACEDATA[0] to TRACEDATA[3] with TRACECLK) or serial on SWO, never both at once. ETM works only in parallel mode; ITM works in either. The trace pins are shared with GPIOs, SWO on the same pin as TRACEDATA[0]. TRACECONFIG sets the trace clock and which signals reach pins; TRACECLK runs at half the trace port clock. Pin speed follows the GPIO drive setting: only S0S1 (the reset default) and H0H1 suit trace, and if signals are too slow all trace pins should be set to H0H1 and left so during the session.

The PMU tracks which supplies and clocks the CPU, memory and peripherals need from moment to moment and starts, stops and switches the regulators and oscillators on its own to keep consumption lowest.
Because the PMU keeps retuning the system, current is given as typical VDD-supply scenarios. Unless a scenario states otherwise, each uses one common set of conditions.

The supply block has on-chip LDO and DC/DC regulators with automatic refresh modes, global System ON and System OFF, per-section RAM power control in every mode, analog or digital pin wake from System OFF, a supervisor for power-on reset, brownout and power failure, a supply output for external circuits, and a separate USB supply.

Supply connects to VDD and VDDH. With VDD and VDDH tied together and both fed, the part runs in Normal voltage mode (VDD range). With supply on VDDH only and VDD fed by nothing else, it runs in High voltage mode (VDDH range). MAINREGSTATUS reports the mode. In the QFN48 package VDD and VDDH are joined inside, so that package runs in Normal voltage mode only.

Two stages, REG0 and REG1, can each run as an LDO or a buck DC/DC. Normal voltage mode uses REG1 alone and switches REG0 off; High voltage mode uses both, REG0 making VDD (set by UICR.REGOUT0), which feeds REG1. The LDOs are on after reset; DCDCEN0 and DCDCEN switch REG0 and REG1 to DC/DC, which turns the matching LDO off. Each DC/DC stage in use needs its external LC filter; enabling a DC/DC without one stops the part working, debug access included, until a filter is fitted. The DC/DC usually lowers total consumption, most of all when the drop across the regulator is large; efficiency varies with supply voltage and load current. In High voltage mode REGOUT0 may not exceed VDDH less VVDDH-VDD. REG1 makes the 1.3 V system supply on DEC4; the REG0 DC/DC switches at DCCH and the REG1 DC/DC at DCC.

GPIO high level equals the voltage on the VDD pin: the supply itself in Normal voltage mode, the REGOUT0 setting in High voltage mode. In High voltage mode REG0's output on the VDD pin may also power external circuits, in System ON and System OFF, provided VDDH stays at least VVDDH-VDD above it; the current allowed (all GPIO current plus current taken from VDD) is IEXT,OFF, IEXT,LOW or IEXT,HIGH and depends on what the chip itself draws.

The supervisor gives a power-on reset when supply arrives, a fixed brownout reset that holds the part in reset while VDD is too low, and an optional power-fail comparator (POF). POFCON enables the comparator and sets its threshold: VPOF on VDD from 1.7 V to 2.8 V, and in High voltage mode VPOFH on VDDH from 2.7 V to 4.2 V. When supply falls below the threshold the POFWARN event fires so firmware can prepare; it also fires if the supply is already below the threshold when the comparator is enabled or the threshold is raised above it. While the warning is enabled and supply is below the threshold the NVMC refuses flash writes. The comparator has hysteresis VPOFHYST and is inactive in System OFF and in System ON while HFCLK is stopped.

USB needs 5 V on VBUS as well as the main supply on VDD or VDDH. A dedicated LDO turns VBUS into the 3.3 V used by the D+ and D- signalling and the D+ pull-up, decoupled at DECUSB; the rest of USBD runs from the main supply. VBUS entering its valid range raises USBDETECTED and leaving it raises USBREMOVED. VBUS arriving during System OFF resets the part into System ON with the VBUS bit set in RESETREAS. With USBD enabled and VBUS present the regulator starts, and USBPWRRDY follows once its worst-case settling time has passed, after which the D+ pull-up may be switched on. USBREGSTATUS shows VBUS detection and regulator readiness at any time. Both the input and the output of the USB regulator need decoupling capacitors.

System OFF is the deepest sleep: core functions are powered down and running tasks end. Writing SYSTEMOFF enters it. Wake sources are the GPIO DETECT signal, the LPCOMP ANADETECT signal, the NFC SENSE signal (wake on field), a valid VBUS (VBUS,DETECT), and a reset; waking always resets the part. RAM sections can be kept according to the retained RAM[n].POWER registers, which start-up code commonly overwrites. All EasyDMA transfers must be finished before entering System OFF. In debug interface mode System OFF is only emulated so that debug, CLOCK, POWER, NVMC, CPU, flash and RAM stay available; since the CPU keeps running, an endless loop should follow the SYSTEMOFF write.

System ON follows power-on reset; the CPU and peripherals are idle or running as software and their activity require, and the PMU switches internal supplies to suit. RESETREAS gives the cause of the last reset or wake. With CPU and peripherals idle the system sits in one of two sub-modes. Constant Latency (CONSTLAT task) keeps base resources on so CPU wake-up and PPI task response stay short and fixed, at higher current. Low-power (LOWPWR task, the default on entering System ON) lets the PMU choose the most efficient supply, with variable wake-up and PPI latency.
RAM[n].POWER sets each section's retention in System OFF (RETENTION field) and its retention and access in System ON (RETENTION and POWER fields). Not retaining RAM lowers current.

RESETREAS records the source of the last reset. Power-on reset holds the part until the supply reaches its minimum operating voltage and the on-chip regulators have started. Pin reset comes from the reset pin set by both PSELRESET registers. Wake from System OFF resets the part, but leaves the DAP alone in debug interface mode. A soft reset comes from SYSRESETREQ in the Cortex-M4 AIRCR or from CTRL-AP RESET. The watchdog resets on time-out. Brownout reset holds the part while VDD is below the BOR threshold. Retained registers keep their value through System OFF and through some resets, depending on the source.

Clocks come from on-chip or crystal oscillators, fast and slow, and are handed out to each module as it asks, with unused branches of the tree gated off. Sources: a 64 MHz on-chip oscillator (HFINT); a 64 MHz crystal oscillator on an external 32 MHz crystal (HFXO); a 32.768 kHz RC oscillator, ±500 ppm (LFRC); a 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator (LFXO); and 32.768 kHz synthesized from the 64 MHz clock (LFSYNT). Firmware can force the crystal oscillators on for fast start, and otherwise the oscillators are started and stopped automatically.

The HFCLK controller supplies HCLK64M (64 MHz CPU clock) and the PCLK1M, PCLK16M and PCLK32M peripheral clocks, from HFINT or HFXO, giving whatever the system requests and dropping to a power-saving state when nothing does. HFINT serves while HFXO is not started. HFCLKSTART starts the HFXO and HFCLKSTOP stops it; HFCLKSTARTED fires after the HFXO power-up time plus the debounce time in HFXODEBOUNCE. The RADIO and LFRC calibration need the HFXO running.

The HFXO runs from a 32 MHz AT-cut crystal in parallel resonance on XC1 and XC2, with ceramic SMD load capacitors C1 and C2 of equal value from each pin to ground. The load seen by the crystal must match its rated load capacitance. Load capacitance, shunt capacitance, ESR and drive level must stay within the HFXO limits CL_HFXO, C0_HFXO, RS_HFXO and PD_HFXO; a crystal below the maximum load and shunt capacitance is preferred, since lower load capacitance shortens start-up and lowers current.

LFCLK comes from LFRC, LFXO or LFSYNT, chosen in LFCLKSRC before LFCLKSTART. With LFXO chosen, LFCLK first runs on LFRC and changes over by itself once the crystal oscillator runs; LFCLKSTARTED marks the LFXO running. LFCLKSTOP stops it, but only once LFCLKSTAT shows LFCLK running, and LFCLKSRC may not be written while LFCLK runs. The controller and every LFCLK source are off in System OFF. LFSYNT is as accurate as HFCLK, so it needs HFCLK on HFXO for accuracy; it saves the 32.768 kHz crystal but keeps HFCLK requested and so raises average current.

LFRC is the default LFCLK source and needs no external parts. LFRCMODE selects normal or ultra-low power (ULP) mode, trading accuracy for current; the oscillator must be stopped to change mode. Its frequency drifts with temperature. The CAL task calibrates it against HFCLK, which must be on HFXO (started by HFCLKSTART); DONE fires when calibration ends. During calibration LFRC may not be stopped and LFRCMODE may not be written.

The calibration timer paces LFRC calibration. CTSTART starts it counting down from CTIV, set in steps of 0.25 s from 0.25 s to 31.75 s and retained; at zero it fires CTTO and stops. After CTSTART it ignores tasks until CTSTARTED, and after CTSTOP until CTSTOPPED. CTSTART while running returns CTSTARTED at once, and CTSTOP while stopped returns CTSTOPPED at once.

When LFCLK must be better than ±500 ppm, the LFXO is used, with a 32.768 kHz crystal on XL1 and XL2 and equal ceramic load capacitors C1 and C2 from each pin to ground, sized to the crystal's rated load. An external clock may replace the crystal: a low-swing signal on XL1 with XL2 grounded, or a rail-to-rail signal on XL1 with XL2 grounded or open.
LFSYNT derives LFCLK from HFCLK and takes on HFCLK's accuracy. It removes the need for a 32.768 kHz crystal at the cost of higher average current, because HFCLK has to stay requested.

The CPU drives a peripheral through configuration and task registers, and learns of its events through event registers and, where enabled, interrupts. Each peripheral owns a 0x1000-byte block (1024 32-bit registers), and its ID follows from its base address: 0x40000000 is ID 0, 0x40001000 ID 1, 0x4001F000 ID 31. Peripherals may share an ID; then they may share registers or resources, work one at a time, or need a set order to switch between them.

Apart from ID 0, peripherals on one ID and base address cannot be used together; only one may be enabled. To switch: disable the old one, remove its PPI connections, clear its interrupts (INTENCLR = 0xFFFFFFFF), configure the new one fully without trusting values left by the old one, then enable it.

Most peripherals have an ENABLE register; their settings, PSEL pin selections above all, go in before enabling, and tasks and events work only once enabled. Some registers use a set/clear trio: the main register followed by SET and CLR, where writing 1 to a bit of SET or CLR sets or clears that bit of the main register, 0 does nothing, and reading either returns the main register. A task fires when firmware writes 1 to it or when a peripheral toggles its signal. An event sets its register when the peripheral signals it, may recur while the register is already 1, and is cleared only by firmware writing 0.

A shortcut ties an event to a task inside one peripheral, like a PPI link but with shorter delay; the pairs are fixed, each enabled by one bit of SHORTS, at most 32 per peripheral. Each peripheral has one interrupt, numbered by its ID, and INTEN, INTENSET and INTENCLR choose which events raise it (reading INTENSET or INTENCLR returns INTEN, and some peripherals lack INTEN itself). Clearing an event or disabling an interrupt takes up to four CPU cycles to act, so a handler that returns sooner may be entered again; reading back a peripheral register, such as the cleared event or INTENCLR, adds the needed delay, and the compiler must not optimise that read away.

The accelerated address resolver checks resolvable private Bluetooth addresses against up to 16 Identity Resolving Keys in real time, so incoming packets can be filtered against known peers. It does not generate such addresses; ECB does that. ADDRPTR points to the start of the packet in RAM, IRKPTR to the key list and SCRATCHPTR to a scratch area of at least 3 bytes, all in Data RAM (elsewhere a HardFault or RAM corruption may follow). NIRK sets how many keys to try, from IRK0 upward. START runs it; it stops at the first key that resolves the 6-byte address (24-bit hash, 24-bit prand) with RESOLVED, or after NIRK keys with NOTRESOLVED, then gives END; EasyDMA is done by those events. It compares addresses without checking the address type. Resolution time grows with the key's place in the list and with RAM traffic from the CPU and other masters. Chained to RADIO, it may start once the six address bytes are in RAM.

Access control lists apply a permission scheme to regions of on-chip flash. There are eight regions, ACL[0] to ACL[7], each set by ADDR (start, on a flash page boundary), SIZE (bytes, a whole number of pages, at most half the flash) and PERM (read and write bits). Protection acts two CPU cycles after the three registers are written, and only with a valid page-aligned ADDR and non-zero SIZE and PERM. Each register can be written once and clears only on a reset, so boot code must set them every time. A blocked access raises a Bus Fault; debugger reads of a read-protected region return zero and its writes to a write-protected region are ignored.

The AES CCM block does Bluetooth LE packet encryption with AES-128 in counter mode plus CBC-MAC, per IETF RFC3610 and NIST SP 800-38C, producing a 4-byte MIC (the MAC in Bluetooth terms). It does three jobs: making a keystream, encrypting a packet and decrypting a packet, and can run in step with RADIO so that each finishes within the packet's air time. EasyDMA reads the key and nonce data (CNFPTR), the input (INPTR) and writes the output (OUTPTR), using a scratch area (SCRATCHPTR); all four must point into Data RAM. The nonce is built in hardware from the CCM data structure.

Each packet needs a fresh keystream, made by KSGEN and finished at ENDKSGEN, from the structure at CNFPTR and the MODE settings, and kept in the scratch area. Default-length packets take a 27-byte keystream; with MODE.LENGTH = Extended, MAXPACKETSIZE sets its length, up to 251 bytes, which must be at least the payload length. With the ENDKSGEN-to-CRYPT shortcut on, INPTR and OUTPTR must be set before KSGEN. Keystream generation takes tkgen.

CRYPT with MODE set to ENCRYPTION reads the plain packet, encrypts the payload, appends the 4-byte MIC, adds 4 to the length field and writes the result at OUTPTR; ENDCRYPT marks completion. With MODE set to DECRYPTION it decrypts, checks the MIC over header (S0) and payload, takes 4 from the length and gives the MIC result in MICSTATUS. Packets with length 0 pass through unchanged and always pass the MIC check; a decrypted packet needs at least 5 bytes (1 payload, 4 MIC), so lengths 1 to 4 give a MIC error. MODE also sets the width of the length field.

For on-the-fly work the MODE data rate must match the radio's; RATEOVERRIDE can change it mid-packet when its task fires. On transmit, OUTPTR equals the radio's PACKETPTR; for short packets KSGEN must fire no later than RADIO START (for example from RADIO READY over PPI) with the ENDKSGEN-to-CRYPT shortcut on, and for long packets earlier, such as at TXEN. On receive, INPTR equals PACKETPTR; for short packets KSGEN fires no later than RADIO START and CRYPT no earlier than the RADIO ADDRESS event. CRYPT at exactly ADDRESS guarantees decryption ends by RADIO END. For long packets KSGEN starts earlier, such as at RXEN. Heavy RAM contention between the CPU and EasyDMA can upset on-the-fly encryption and raises ERROR. EasyDMA is done at ENDKSGEN and ENDCRYPT.

The general-purpose comparator compares VIN+ with VIN-, over an input range of 0 V to VDD. VIN+ is any of AIN0 to AIN7, chosen by PSEL. In differential mode VIN- is another AIN pin (EXTREFSEL), with optional hysteresis VDIFFHYST from HYST. In single-ended mode VIN- comes from a 64-level reference ladder on VREF, which is VDD, an AIN pin (AREF via EXTREFSEL) or the internal 1.2 V, 1.8 V or 2.4 V reference (REFSEL); VREF must sit at least VVDD-VREF below VDD. Low-power, normal and high-speed modes trade current against response time. Events: UP when VIN+ rises above VIN-, DOWN when it falls below, CROSS on either, and READY when the core and any internal reference are ready. Once ENABLE is set, START starts it and STOP stops it; READY follows START after tINT_REF,START with an internal reference or tCOMP,START with an external one. SAMPLE copies the present output to RESULT (1 = ABOVE, VIN+ > VIN-). The chosen analog pins are taken over when the comparator is enabled; not every AIN may be available on each input multiplexer in every package.
Set PSEL, MODE and EXTREFSEL before enabling. With HYST on, the output goes BELOW when VIN+ drops under VIN- minus VDIFFHYST/2 and ABOVE when it rises over VIN- plus VDIFFHYST/2.

Set PSEL, MODE, REFSEL, EXTREFSEL and TH before enabling. TH sets THUP and THDOWN, which take VUP and VDOWN from the ladder. While the output is BELOW, VIN- is VUP; once ABOVE, VIN- switches to VDOWN, so VUP above VDOWN gives hysteresis of the order of VDIFFHYST. HYST is ignored in this mode.

Arm TrustZone CryptoCell 310 is the security subsystem: root of trust and crypto services. It offers a TRNG to FIPS 140-2, BSI AIS-31 and NIST 800-90B; a PRNG on the AES engine to NIST 800-90A; RSA signature verification and key generation up to 2048-bit keys with PKCS#1 v2.1/v1.5; ECC over NIST FIPS 186-4 prime curves P-192 to P-521, SEC 2 secp160r1 to secp521r1, Koblitz secp160k1 to secp256k1, BrainpoolP256r1, Ed25519 and Curve25519, with ECDH and ECDSA; SRP up to 3072-bit; SHA-1 and SHA-2 up to 256 bits with HMAC; AES-128 in ECB, CBC, CMAC/CBC-MAC, CTR and CCM/CCM*; and ChaCha20/Poly1305 with 128- or 256-bit keys in AEAD mode. It is meant to be used through the libraries in Nordic's SDK, which switch it on and off as needed; its register interface may change without notice.

ENABLE (CRYPTOCELL base 0x5002A000, offset 0x500) powers the subsystem; while it is on the part does not enter System ON IDLE. Each engine has its own clock, gated through the MISC interface (AES_CLK, HASH_CLK, PKA_CLK, DMA_CLK, CHACHA_CLK, status in CLK_STATUS) or, for the RNG engine, RNG_CLK; an engine's registers answer only while its clock runs. For lowest power: make sure no task is pending, clear RNG_ICR and ICR, then clear ENABLE. A typical operation enables the subsystem, clocks the engines, picks the flow in CRYPTO_CTL, sets up the engine and its key, optionally sets up DMA, starts the job, waits for the interrupt and checks status.

Internal storage keeps the lifecycle state, lock bits and the 128-bit device root key KDR while the subsystem is disabled; any reset erases it. HOST_IOT_LCS sets the lifecycle state, write-once per reset: DebugEnable (0) or Secure (2), with read-only LCS_IS_VALID turning Valid once a valid value is stored. In DebugEnable the KDR registers can be rewritten and the TRNG output can be overridden by writing EHR_DATA; in Secure, EHR_DATA is read-only and random.

HOST_CRYPTOKEY_SEL picks the AES key: the RTL key KPRTL, the device root key KDR, or a session key. KPRTL is fixed in hardware, the same for every device of one part code, usable without being readable, and can be locked until reset with HOST_IOT_KPRTL_LOCK, after which a request for it gives a zero key. KDR is a 128-bit key normally loaded at boot by an immutable bootloader into HOST_IOT_KDR0 to HOST_IOT_KDR3 and kept until reset; it is held while HOST_IOT_KDR0 reads back Retained, and it should be protected with ACL. Session keys are written in clear by the CPU into an engine's write-only key registers in the set order: AES takes 128-bit keys, CHACHA 128- or 256-bit keys, and each engine keeps its last key until disabled, engine reset or device reset. Asymmetric keys go into PKA SRAM with the data.

Two private memories are fitted: 4 kB of PKA SRAM and 2 kB of RNG SRAM. The DIN and DOUT DMA engines move data in and out of the engines, at most 2^16-1 bytes per transfer; a larger setting needs the engine reset (DIN_SW_RESET or DOUT_SW_RESET) before it works again. Data outside RAM must be copied into RAM first. In bypass mode (DMA_CLK on, CRYPTO_CTL set to bypass, destination then source written) the DMA works as a plain memory mover, with progress in DOUT_DMA_MEM_BUSY or the DOUT_TO_MEM interrupt. Writing SRC_MEM_SIZE starts a DIN transfer from SRC_MEM_ADDR; DST_MEM_ADDR and DST_MEM_SIZE set the DOUT destination. DOUT_SW_RESET takes 4 CPU cycles.

The subsystem raises its interrupt when a job completes; IRR shows which source asked. Clear the source in ICR to drop the line; IMR masks sources. If IRR shows RNG_INT, clear the RNG engine's bit in RNG_ICR before clearing ICR.

The AES engine follows FIPS 197 for 128-bit keys, encrypting, decrypting, signing and verifying in ECB, CBC, CBC-MAC, CMAC, CTR, CCM and CCM*. Key words go in ascending order, AES_KEY_0[0] to AES_KEY_0[3]. A typical job: enable the subsystem, turn on AES and DMA clocks, wait for CRYPTO_BUSY idle, set CRYPTO_CTL to AES, set AES_CONTROL, load key and IV, set the DOUT destination, then write the DIN source and size to start, and wait for the DOUT_TO_MEM interrupt. A write to the zero-size CMAC register forces a CMAC of an empty message, read from AES_IV_0.

The CHACHA engine accelerates the ChaCha stream cipher with keys up to 256 bits in 8, 12 or 20 rounds (20 by default); with Poly1305 on the PKA engine it forms the RFC7539 AEAD construction. Key words go in ascending order, CHACHA_KEY[0] to [3] for 128-bit keys and on to [7] for 256-bit keys. The job flow matches AES with CHACHA_CLK, a nonce in CHACHA_IV and CHACHA_CONTROL set for a new message. Control bits can reverse word and byte order of input and output and the order of matrix quarters, and CHACHA_DEBUG shows the engine state (idle, init, rounds, final).

The HASH engine implements FIPS 180-4 SHA-1, SHA-224 and SHA-256. The initial hash values go in descending order from HASH_H[7] (SHA-256 and SHA-224) or HASH_H[4] (SHA-1) down to HASH_H[0]. A job enables HASH and DMA clocks, waits for HASH_BUSY idle, clears interrupts, sets CRYPTO_CTL to hash, picks the mode in HASH_CONTROL, enables padding (HASH_PAD, HASH_PAD_AUTO), loads the initial values, starts the DIN transfer, then waits for HASH_BUSY idle; the digest is in HASH_H[0] to HASH_H[7]. HASH_ENDIANNESS selects little-endian (default) or big-endian data and padding.

The public key accelerator is a modular big-number ALU for RSA and ECC with operands of 128 to 3136 bits: modular exponentiation and inversion, add, subtract, increment, decrement, multiply and divide (modular or plain) and logic (AND, OR, XOR, shifts). It works on 32 virtual registers R0 to R31 placed in PKA SRAM by MEMORY_MAP; N (modulus, R0 by default), Np (Barrett inverse modulus, R1), T0 (R30) and T1 (R31) are special and can be remapped with N_NP_T0_T1_ADDR. Each register must be 64-bit aligned and hold the largest operand plus 64 zeroed bits. Writing OPCODE starts an operation, naming the operation, result register REG_R, operands REG_A and REG_B (or constants via CONST_A, CONST_B) and an operand length LEN chosen from PKA_L. The pipeline is one opcode deep: PKA_PIPE shows when the next can be loaded, PKA_DONE when all are finished, or the PKA interrupt can be unmasked. PKA SRAM is not memory mapped and is reached through PKA_SRAM_WADDR/WDATA and PKA_SRAM_RADDR/RDATA with auto-increment; PKA_SRAM_WCLEAR clears the write buffer between writing and reading. All access to it is blocked while the engine runs. The memory map should be rewritten after reset.

The RNG engine gathers entropy from the jitter of a free-running on-chip ring oscillator, meeting FIPS 140-2, BSI AIS-31 and NIST SP 800-90B, and seeds a CTR DRBG (NIST SP 800-90A) run on the AES engine in counter mode. TRNG_CONFIG picks one of four ring lengths, ROSC1 (shortest) to ROSC4, and SAMPLE_CNT must hold the matching device-specific sample count from FICR TRNG90B.ROSC1 to ROSC4, the CPU cycles between samples. Setup: clock on (RNG_CLK), reset (RNG_SW_RESET), clock on again and write SAMPLE_CNT starting with the shortest ring, read it back, set TRNG_CONFIG, enable NOISE_SOURCE, then wait for EHR_VALID_INT in RNG_ISR, which marks 192 random bits ready in EHR_DATA[0] to EHR_DATA[5], read in ascending order. If any of the three test error interrupts in RNG_ISR fires (autocorrelation, CRNGT or VNC), restart from the reset with the next longer ring. The shortest working ring finishes soonest and keeps the oscillator off longest. Reading the top EHR_DATA word clears TRNG_VALID and starts a new 192-bit collection.

The 2 kB RNG SRAM can hold a large pool of entropy. It is not memory mapped: single words go through SRAM_ADDR, SRAM_DATA and SRAM_DATA_READY (CRYPTOCELL enabled, address auto-incremented), and larger blocks through the DIN and DOUT DMA engines. On reading, the first SRAM_DATA value is stale and is discarded. At the last address the increment stops and further accesses repeat on the last word.

Samples pass a von Neumann corrector, then a continuous random number test and an autocorrelation test. The corrector flags VNC_ERR_INT after 32 identical bits in a row and otherwise outputs about one bit per four sampled. The continuous test flags CRNGT_ERR_INT when two consecutive 16-bit blocks match. The autocorrelation test discards biased output and records it in AUTOCORR_STATISTIC; after four biased results in a row it flags AUTOCORR_ERR_INT and the TRNG stops until RNG_SW_RESET.

The CTL interface sets the flow in CRYPTO_CTL and shows busy status (CRYPTO_BUSY, HASH_BUSY), with a free CONTEXT_ID register. The DIN engine can also take data written by the CPU into DIN_BUFFER (DIN_CPU_DATA gives the byte count, DIN_WRITE_ALIGN marks the last write when the size is not a multiple of 4) and its FIFO can be reset; the DOUT engine offers DOUT_BUFFER for CPU reads, with DOUT_READ_ALIGN for the last word. The HOST_RGF interface holds the interrupt registers, the lifecycle state and the key selection and root-key registers, normally set by an immutable bootloader so the application can use KDR without seeing it.

The AES ECB block encrypts one 128-bit block with a 128-bit key (encryption only), for uses such as hashing, signatures and keystream generation. STARTECB loads key and cleartext by EasyDMA from the structure at ECBDATAPTR, which must be in Data RAM, and ENDECB fires once the ciphertext is written back; STOPECB aborts. ECB shares its AES core with CCM and AAR at lowest priority: a conflict aborts it with ERRORECB. EasyDMA is done at ENDECB or ERRORECB.

The event generator units let firmware or the PPI trigger events and interrupts, for example to hand work from a high-priority context to a lower one, or between any priorities. Six instances, EGU0 to EGU5 (0x40014000 to 0x40019000), each have their own interrupt vector and 16 trigger/event pairs: TASKS_TRIGGER[n] raises EVENTS_TRIGGERED[n].

GPIOs are grouped in ports of up to 32 pins; the nRF52840 has P0 (0x50000000) and P1 (0x50000300), and the count per port depends on the package. Each pin's PIN_CNF[n] (retained) sets direction, drive, pull-up or pull-down, sensing, input buffer connection and, on some pins, analog input. Any pin can be assigned to a peripheral, used by PPI and GPIOTE, and set to wake the part on a high or low level.

A pin's SENSE field makes it watch for a high or a low level; a match raises that pin's DETECT. By default (DETECTMODE) all pins' DETECT signals are ORed into the port's DETECT, which works in System ON and System OFF and is used by POWER to leave System OFF and by GPIOTE for the PORT event. A pin should sit at a non-triggering level when sensing is enabled: if it already matches, DETECT goes high at once, and a PORT event follows if DETECT was low. Each pin's DETECT also sets its bit in LATCH, which only a CPU write of 1 to that bit clears, and not while the pin's DETECT is still high. LDETECT is high while any LATCH bit is 1, and a clear that leaves a bit set makes a new rising edge on it. DETECTMODE can route LDETECT to the port DETECT instead. LATCH can be read at any time to see which pins have matched, even if the condition has passed.

operation.topic: GPIO input buffer and analog pins
operation.text: The input buffer can be disconnected to save power on pins not used as inputs; it must be connected for IN to read correctly and for sensing to work. Peripherals can override a pin's output and configuration and read its analog or digital input. An input held between VIL and VIH draws extra current, so external circuits should not leave a digital input there for long.

GPIOTE (0x40006000) ties pins to the task and event system through 8 channels, each bound to one pin by CONFIG[n].PSEL. In task mode a channel drives its pin from SET[n] (high), CLR[n] (low) and OUT[n] (set, clear or toggle, chosen by CONFIG[n].POLARITY), starting from the OUTINIT level, and the pin is then an output whose GPIO OUT value and direction are ignored. In event mode the pin becomes an input and IN[n] fires on a rising edge, a falling edge or any change. With MODE Disabled the pin falls back to its GPIO PIN_CNF setting. If tasks clash in the same clock cycle, OUT wins over CLR, and CLR over SET; so MODE=Task with POLARITY=None differs from Disabled, since SET or CLR at the same moment as OUT leaves the pin unchanged. A pin may belong to only one channel at a time. Pin changes can be detected at low power in System ON and System OFF.

PORT fires on the rising edge of the GPIO DETECT signal from any number of sensing pins. It needs no clock or other costly resource, so it can wake the CPU from WFI or WFE at the lowest System ON current. If DETECT is still high when the system goes to System ON IDLE it will not wake it, so clear all DETECT sources first; with LATCH as the source, any bit left set makes a new rising edge. Entering System OFF with DETECT high causes an immediate wake-up reset. To avoid stray PORT interrupts while setting up: disable the PORT interrupt (INTENCLR.PORT), set PIN_CNF[n].SENSE, clear EVENTS_PORT, then re-enable it (INTENSET.PORT).

The I2S block (one instance, base 0x40025000) carries digital audio in standard two-channel I2S framing or in left- or right-aligned framing, as master or slave, with transmit and receive able to run at once. Samples are 8, 16 or 24 bits wide and move between pins and RAM by EasyDMA, with no CPU work per sample. A low-jitter master-clock generator sets the sample rate. Its five signals are MCK, LRCK, SCK, SDIN and SDOUT.

The master drives LRCK and SCK and the slave takes them. Outgoing bits change on SDOUT at the falling edge of SCK; incoming bits on SDIN are taken at the rising edge; the most significant bit goes first. TX and RX are switched on separately (CONFIG.TXEN, CONFIG.RXEN) in either mode.

The START task begins streaming. With TX on, a TXPTRUPD event comes each time RXTXD.MAXCNT words have been sent; with RX on, an RXPTRUPD event comes each time that many words have arrived. A word holds one or more samples. STOP ends the transfer, stops the MCK generator and gives the STOPPED event.

LRCK (word clock) marks the frames, each frame being one left and one right sample, so its frequency equals the audio sample rate. In I2S format the left sample is sent while LRCK is low and the right while it is high; in Aligned format the left sample goes while LRCK is high and the right while it is low. As master, LRCK is MCK divided by CONFIG.RATIO. LRCK changes around the falling edge of SCK.

SCK has one pulse per data bit on SDIN and SDOUT. As master it is derived from MCK at 2 × LRCK × sample width, and its falling edge lines up with each LRCK change. As slave it comes from the external master.

MCK is the root clock for LRCK and SCK in master mode, made by the internal MCK generator, which must be on in master mode and may also be turned on in slave mode to give an external master a clock. CONFIG.MCKEN enables the generator; START and STOP run and halt it. In master mode CONFIG.RATIO and CONFIG.SWIDTH fix both LRCK and SCK, and two rules hold: SCK may not be faster than MCK (RATIO at least 2 × SWIDTH), and RATIO must be a whole multiple of 2 × SWIDTH. MCK can be brought out on the PSEL.MCK pin for parts that need an external master clock. In slave mode the block does not use MCK.

CONFIG.SWIDTH sets the sample width in memory; as master it also sets the bits per half-frame, and as slave it governs padding and trimming. All samples, left and right, TX and RX, share one width. CONFIG.FORMAT places the data against the LRCK edges: in I2S format the first bit of a half-frame is sampled at the second rising SCK edge after the LRCK edge, in Aligned format at the first. CONFIG.ALIGN (left or right) applies only to decoding SDIN; SDOUT is always left-justified, starting each half-frame with the MSB. As master the half-frame is exactly the sample width, so alignment makes no difference. As slave the frame may hold more or fewer SCK pulses than the width. Left-aligned with extra pulses: SDIN bits after the LSB are dropped and SDOUT sends zeros after the LSB. Left-aligned with too few pulses: both directions lose LSBs first. Right-aligned with extra pulses: SDIN bits ahead of the MSB are dropped, and SDOUT pads zeros after the LSB. Right-aligned with too few pulses: received data is sign-extended to the sample width in memory, and sent data loses LSBs first.

TXD.PTR and RXD.PTR give the RAM buffers; each is read or written only while its direction is enabled. Both pointers are double-buffered, and the hardware takes the new values every RXTXD.MAXCNT words, raising TXPTRUPD and RXPTRUPD as it does. A pointer outside Data RAM while its direction is on can cause a HardFault or corrupt memory. Since TX and RX move equal numbers of samples, one count, RXTXD.MAXCNT, sizes both buffers, in 32-bit words. Each word packs four 8-bit, two 16-bit or one 24-bit sample, the last right-aligned and sign-extended to 32 bits. In stereo (CONFIG.CHANNELS=Stereo) samples sit in memory as left/right pairs, left in the lower bits, for both TX and RX. In mono (CONFIG.CHANNELS Left or Right) only one channel's received samples are stored, packed consecutively; on TX each sample read from memory goes out on both left and right.

A typical start: set the CONFIG registers (RX and TX enable, MCK enable, MCKFREQ, RATIO, SWIDTH, ALIGN, FORMAT, CHANNELS); route MCK, SCK, LRCK, SDOUT and SDIN through their PSEL registers; give TXD.PTR, RXD.PTR and the buffer size; set ENABLE to 1; trigger START; then on each TXPTRUPD or RXPTRUPD event load the next buffer pointer and clear the event. MCKFREQ 32MDIV8 (4 MHz) with RATIO 256X gives 15.625 kHz.

PSEL.MCK, PSEL.SCK, PSEL.LRCK, PSEL.SDIN and PSEL.SDOUT name the pins (pin 0 to 31, port 0 or 1, and a connect bit). The block takes the pins when ENABLE is set and sets their direction itself, over the GPIO setting. To hold defined levels in System OFF and while the block is disabled, the pins must also be set in GPIO.

The low-power comparator (base 0x40013000) checks one of the analog inputs AIN0 to AIN7 (VIN+, chosen by PSEL) against a reference (VIN−): one of two external references on AIN0 or AIN1 (EXTREFSEL), or a 15-step internal ladder in sixteenths of VDD, VDD × 1/16 up to VDD × 15/16 (REFSEL). Inputs range from 0 to VDD. Hysteresis can be added (HYST, off by default). PSEL, REFSEL, EXTREFSEL and HYST must be set before ENABLE. It cannot be started while COMP is in use: only one of the two comparators runs at a time.

START begins it; after tSTARTUP it raises READY and its output is valid. Each upward crossing of VIN+ past VIN− gives UP and CROSS, each downward crossing DOWN and CROSS. With hysteresis on, the thresholds move to VIN− + VHYST/2 going up and VIN− − VHYST/2 going down. STOP halts it. The SAMPLE task copies the present output into RESULT. It works in System ON and System OFF once enabled; going to System OFF while a READY event is still due is not allowed. While enabled its registers, ENABLE included, are retained, but a wake from System OFF resets them all.

It wakes the device from System OFF through the ANADETECT signal, which can follow any of the UP, DOWN or CROSS sources (ANADETECT register). Such a wake produces no event, only ANADETECT; RESETREAS shows the LPCOMP as the cause. It can also act as an analog wake source in System ON.

It shares analog circuitry with the SAADC; both may run at once but not on the same input pin. It also shares registers with the other peripherals on its ID. It must be stopped before ENABLE is cleared, or behaviour is unpredictable. The selected input and reference pins are taken over when ENABLE is set.

The memory watch unit (base 0x40020000) raises events when the CPU reads or writes inside chosen address ranges of Data RAM or peripheral space, useful for debugging or for catching faults in the field. It has four configurable regions REGION[0..3] and two fixed peripheral regions PREGION[0..1]. Each region has inclusive, byte-aligned START and END addresses (END not below START) and its own write-access and read-access events, each able to raise a normal interrupt or an NMI. It sees only CPU accesses to Data RAM and peripherals, not EasyDMA, and needs two HCLK cycles to detect an access and raise the event.

Each PREGION is split into 32 equal subregions SR[0..31], all excluded by default and included through the SUBS register; an excluded subregion never triggers. Read and write watching is chosen for the PREGION as a whole (PRGNiRA, PRGNiWA in REGIONEN), not per subregion, and PERREGION[0..1].SUBSTATWA and SUBSTATRA tell which subregions caused the event. REGION[0..3] are enabled for read or write watching by RGNiRA and RGNiWA. REGIONENSET and REGIONENCLR change several regions in one write.

The NFC tag peripheral (base 0x40005000) is an NFC Forum NFC-A listener: a 13.56 MHz AM receiver and load modulator at 106 kbps on the NFC1 and NFC2 pins. In hardware it assembles and takes apart NFC-A frames (start and end of frame, parity, CRC), times the reply frame, and runs anticollision automatically. Frame data moves to and from RAM by EasyDMA, and an event marks each complete frame sent or received. With suitable software it serves as an NFC Forum NFC-A listening device.

In SENSE mode a low-power field detector watches for a reader, in System ON or System OFF. In System ON it gives FIELDDETECTED when the antenna energy rises past a threshold and FIELDLOST when the field can no longer carry communication. In System OFF it wakes the device by a reset (RESETREAS shows NFCT as the cause); entering System OFF with a field already present resets the device at once. Because a reset disables NFCT, the reset handler must activate and configure it again.

The HFXO must run before NFCT enters the ACTIVATED state; ACTIVATE also calibrates the peripheral. The HFXO may be stopped while NFCT sits in SENSE mode. If the HFXO already runs in SENSE mode, the FIELDDETECTED_ACTIVATE shortcut can be used.

Tasks and events move NFCT between states and let software follow them: DISABLE, SENSE (SENSE_FIELD), then after ACTIVATE the activated states IDLERU, IDLE, READY_A, READY_A*, SLEEP_A and ACTIVE_A, in which ENABLERXDATA leads to RECEIVE and STARTTX to TRANSMIT. GOIDLE and GOSLEEP send it to IDLE or SLEEP_A. With automatic collision resolution off, ACTIVATE leads through IDLERU straight to ACTIVE_A. FIELDLOST does not occur in SENSE mode. SENSE issued with the field still present gives no FIELDDETECTED. If FIELDDETECTED is cleared before ACTIVATE, it reappears after ACTIVATE; the FIELDDETECTED_ACTIVATE shortcut avoids that.

The antenna takes two pins shared with GPIO. UICR NFCPINS.PROTECT, reloaded at every reset, decides their use. With PROTECT=NFC a protection circuit is on that shorts the pins together if they differ by more than about 2 V, guarding against a strong field, and GPIO use of the pins is off. With PROTECT=Disabled there is no such protection and NFCT never leaves DISABLE. Used as GPIO, the two pins have higher capacitance (CPAD_NFC) and leak between each other when driven to different levels (INFC_LEAK); they should be set to the same level before entering a power-saving mode.

A single pointer, PACKETPTR, serves receive and transmit, and EasyDMA does one direction at a time. RXFRAMESTART and RXFRAMEEND bracket writing a received frame to RAM; TXFRAMESTART and TXFRAMEEND bracket reading a frame to send. If both are requested together, transmit wins. Starting a transmit while a received frame is being written, or any EasyDMA operation while another runs, is unpredictable, so wait for TXFRAMEEND or RXFRAMEEND first. MAXLEN caps the bytes read or written; a frame longer than MAXLEN is cut short, and on receive the OVERRUN bit of FRAMESTATUS.RX is set and RXERROR fires. RXD.AMOUNT and TXD.AMOUNT count bytes and bits without SoF, EoF and parity; RXD.AMOUNT includes CRC, TXD.AMOUNT does not. A new receive pointer takes effect only through ENABLERXDATA. PACKETPTR outside Data RAM can cause a hard fault or RAM corruption. For the next frame, PACKETPTR, MAXLEN and the frame configuration of the other direction may be updated as soon as STARTED for the frame in progress arrives; changing the current direction's frame configuration mid-frame is unpredictable. On air the least significant bit of the least significant byte goes first, and bytes lie in RAM in rising address order.

For transmit, in ACTIVE_A, software sets PACKETPTR and MAXLEN (matching the frame) and triggers STARTTX; STARTED shows both were captured. The assembler reads TXD.AMOUNT.TXDATABYTES bytes, plus one more when TXDATABITS is above zero, and sends 8 × TXDATABYTES + TXDATABITS bits, framed as TXD.FRAMECONFIG says: optional SoF, parity bits and CRC computed on the fly, which covers short, standard and bit-oriented SDD frame types. Bytes go out in RAM order, each LSB first (b0 before b1). DISCARDMODE picks whether the spare bits of a partial byte are dropped from the start of the first byte or the end of the last. With parity on and DiscardStart, a parity bit follows the partial first byte; no parity follows a partial last byte.

For receive, in ACTIVE_A, software sets PACKETPTR and MAXLEN and triggers ENABLERXDATA; STARTED shows they were captured. RXFRAMESTART comes as a frame begins and data is written to RAM. Parity, SoF and EoF are checked and removed as RXD.FRAMECONFIG says; CRC bytes, if CRC is on, are checked and also written to RAM. At EoF, RXFRAMEEND fires and RXD.AMOUNT gives the bytes and bits received. Content beyond framing, parity and CRC is not interpreted. Only 86 µs may separate the end of one frame from the start of the next, so the pointer, MAXLEN and ENABLERXDATA must be ready in time; a PPI link from TXFRAMEEND to ENABLERXDATA is recommended.

A counter tracks 13.56 MHz carrier periods since the end of the last received frame's EoF, corrected for the last data bit as NFC-A requires, so a reply goes out at a set time. FRAMEDELAYMODE=Window: STARTTX before FRAMEDELAYMIN waits until FRAMEDELAYMIN, and STARTTX between FRAMEDELAYMIN and FRAMEDELAYMAX sends at once. ExactVal: STARTTX before FRAMEDELAYMAX waits until FRAMEDELAYMAX. WindowGrid: as Window, but the start falls on the NFC-A listen bit grid (slots of 128 carrier periods). If the counter reaches FRAMEDELAYMAX with no STARTTX, ERROR fires with FRAMEDELAYTIMEOUT in ERRORSTATUS, which can also happen when no reply is due, and after commands handled by automatic collision resolution that need no reply. FRAMEDELAYMIN and FRAMEDELAYMAX should be changed only before STARTTX.

Automatic anticollision is on by default and recommended, saving power and software; AUTOCOLRESCONFIG.MODE turns it off, after which every command arrives by EasyDMA. SENSRES and SELRES must be set first, and by the ID size in SENSRES: NFCID1_LAST for a 4-byte ID; NFCID1_2ND_LAST and NFCID1_LAST for 7 bytes; NFCID1_3RD_LAST, NFCID1_2ND_LAST and NFCID1_LAST for 10 bytes. FICR NFC.TAGHEADER0..3 hold a valid NFCID1 to fill them. Hardware handles IDLE through ACTIVE_A; other states are software's. AUTOCOLRESSTARTED marks the start, SELECTED arrival in ACTIVE_A, COLLISION a failure. Other events, ERROR and RXERROR among them, may appear meanwhile; software should heed only COLLISION, SELECTED and FIELDLOST, and turn off unwanted shortcuts and PPI links during resolution. Frames with CRC or parity errors in ACTIVE_A restart resolution unless the feature is turned off in ACTIVE_A. SLP_REQ is handled automatically but, having no reply, causes an ERROR with FRAMEDELAYTIMEOUT that software ignores until SELECTED and then clears.

When activated, an amplitude regulator keeps the antenna pin swing within its limit. The antenna coil connects differentially across NFC1 and NFC2, and two external capacitors, one from each pin to ground, tune it to 13.56 MHz. The capacitance on NFC1 and NFC2 must be matched. A 2 µH antenna needs about 130 pF per pin.
In a strong field, current can flow backwards into the supply through parasitic diodes and ESD structures. A battery that cannot accept reverse current needs a series diode between it and the device.

The PDM interface takes pulse-density-modulated audio from external front ends such as digital microphones. It drives the PDM clock (CLK) and reads one data line (DIN) carrying one channel or a left/right pair, so up to two microphones share the input. Hardware decimation filters turn the bitstreams into 16-bit PCM at a 16 kHz output rate, with a PDM_CLK to sample-rate ratio of 64 or 80, and EasyDMA writes the samples to RAM so streaming can be continuous.
PDMCLKCTRL sets the PDM clock frequency. The clock generator adds no jitter to the chosen HFCLK source; using the crystal as HFCLK is recommended but not required.

By default the left microphone's bits are taken on the falling edge of PDM_CLK and the right's on the rising edge; MODE.EDGE swaps them. Each stream is filtered to 16-bit PCM and decimated by 64 or 80 (RATIO). MODE.OPERATION chooses Stereo (left and right samples alternating in RAM) or Mono (left only). The application keeps streaming going by updating the pointer as each buffer fills. START and STOP run and halt acquisition; STOP takes effect after the current frame, then STOPPED shows all activity, DMA included, is over. Restarting before STOPPED is unpredictable.

Each channel's filter is followed by a digital volume control set by GAINL and GAINR, in 0.5 dB steps, spanning −20 dB to +20 dB about the default GPDM,default. To reach a target level, add the module's default gain to the gain of the microphone and acoustic path (an attenuation counts as negative) and shift GAINL and GAINR by that sum, keeping within MinGain and MaxGain. Example: for 2500 RMS 16-bit output from a 1 kHz 90 dBA tone into a −26 dBFS microphone, with only the module contributing, the gain is set to −GPDM,default; with GPDM,default = 3.2 dB the nearest step is 3.0 dB.

SAMPLE.PTR sets the RAM address; outside Data RAM a transfer can cause a HardFault or RAM corruption. Samples are stored little-endian. SAMPLE.MAXCNT sets the buffer length in 16-bit samples, so the RAM used is always SAMPLE.MAXCNT × 2 bytes, holding left/right pairs in stereo or left samples only in mono; for the same count a stereo buffer covers half the time of a mono one. START begins acquisition once SAMPLE.PTR and SAMPLE.MAXCNT are written. The filters need time to settle and the microphone may give transients, so the first samples, typically about 50, can be wrong and should be discarded. SAMPLE.PTR is double-buffered: after STARTED the next address may be written. When a buffer is full, END fires and acquisition carries on into the next buffer with a new STARTED.

PSEL.CLK and PSEL.DIN route the two signals; with CONNECT=Disconnected the signal reaches no pin and the block will not work. These settings apply only while the block is enabled and are kept only in System ON; when disabled the pins act as ordinary GPIO under their OUT bit and PIN_CNF. The pins should be set up in GPIO before enabling, and kept so while a PDM device is connected, so they stay driven correctly if the block is briefly disabled or the device enters System OFF. Only one peripheral may drive a given pin.

The programmable peripheral interconnect (base 0x4001F000) lets an event in one peripheral trigger a task in another with no CPU involvement, giving exact timing between peripherals. A channel has one event end point (EEP) and a task end point (TEP), given as the addresses of the event and task registers, and each TEP has a fork (FORK[n].TEP) that triggers a second task at the same moment. Signals on each channel are synchronised to the 16 MHz clock: events already synchronous to it are delayed one period, others up to one period. Peripheral shortcuts (SHORTS) bypass this and are not delayed. One event can drive several tasks through several channels, and one task can be driven by several events.

Channels are switched on singly through CHEN, CHENSET and CHENCLR, or in groups through each group's ENABLE and DISABLE tasks after the group's membership is set (CHG[n]). There are six groups (CHG[0..5]). The group tasks are ordinary tasks and can themselves be TEPs. If a channel in groups m and n sees CHG[m].EN and CHG[n].DIS at the same time, enable wins. Channels 20 to 31 are fixed in hardware: the CPU cannot change their EEP or TEP, but they can be enabled, disabled and grouped like the others, and their fork TEPs stay programmable.

Four PWM modules, PWM0 to PWM3 (bases 0x4001C000, 0x40021000, 0x40022000, 0x4002D000), each drive up to four GPIO outputs OUT[0..3] from one 15-bit counter, so a module's channels share a period but each has its own duty cycle and polarity. Pulses are edge- or centre-aligned. Duty-cycle values come from sequences in RAM read by EasyDMA without the CPU and without glitches; polarity, duty and even the period can change every PWM period, and sequences can repeat or chain in loops.

The counter's top is COUNTERTOP and its clock PWM_CLK comes from PRESCALER. MODE picks counting up (edge-aligned) or up-and-down (centre-aligned). Bit 15 of each 16-bit RAM value sets polarity: 1 is FallingEdge (the output starts high and goes low within the period), 0 RisingEdge (the reverse); bits 14:0 are the compare value. In up mode the counter returns to zero at COUNTERTOP and the output flips. With FallingEdge polarity, a compare of 0 holds the output low, a compare equal to COUNTERTOP holds it high, and a COUNTERTOP below the compare gives no edges with the output held high. In up-and-down mode the counter turns at COUNTERTOP and the output flips again when the compare is met on the way down. The compare registers are internal and loaded only through the decoder. COUNTERTOP can be written at any time; with DECODER.LOAD=WaveForm it is ignored and comes from RAM instead.

The decoder reads 16-bit values from RAM by EasyDMA into the compare registers. DECODER.LOAD sets the layout: Common (one value for all four channels), Grouped (one value per pair, OUT[0..1] and OUT[2..3]), Single (one value per channel), or WaveForm (three channel values then a COUNTERTOP value, so up to three channels, OUT[0] to OUT[2], with a period that can change every cycle, for arbitrary waveforms such as LED lighting). SEQ[n].REFRESH = N loads a new value every (N+1)th period; 0 loads one each period if the minimum period allows. With DECODER.MODE=NextStep, REFRESH and ENDDELAY are ignored and each NEXTSTEP task loads the next value on the next period.

Two sequences, SEQ[0] and SEQ[1], each have a RAM pointer SEQ[n].PTR (outside RAM a transfer can cause a HardFault or RAM corruption) and a length SEQ[n].CNT in half-words: Grouped needs one per group and Single one per channel. A sequence in use must have CNT above zero. If PWM is not running, SEQSTART[n] loads the first value and starts it; SEQSTARTED[n] fires once the first value is read and running. With LOOP.CNT=0 the sequence plays once, SEQEND[n] comes after the last value starts, and the output holds the last value. With LOOP.CNT above zero the module plays SEQ[0], its ENDDELAY, SEQ[1], its ENDDELAY, and again, LOOP.CNT times, starting from whichever sequence was started and always ending with SEQ[1]'s delay; LOOPSDONE then fires, possibly in either order with SEQEND[1], and the last value is held (REFRESH and ENDDELAY are not applied at that end). STOP, at any time, halts generation at the end of the current period, gives STOPPED and returns the pins to their GPIO OUT idle level; only SEQSTART[n] restarts it. If the period is shorter than the time EasyDMA needs to fetch a value, the previous compare value is repeated, so output stays glitch-free.

PSEL.OUT[n] routes each channel; with CONNECT=Disconnected the signal reaches no pin. The settings apply while the module is enabled and generating and are kept only in System ON. The pins should be set as outputs in GPIO before enabling, with the idle level in GPIO OUT, and kept so while a PWM load is connected, so they stay driven after STOP, while the module is briefly disabled, or in System OFF. Only one peripheral may drive a given pin.

The quadrature decoder (base 0x40012000) decodes the phase A and phase B outputs of an off-chip mechanical or optical incremental encoder. It samples both inputs at a fixed period (SAMPLEPER) and compares each sample pair with the previous one; the phase that changes first gives the direction. Both changing at once is an invalid double transition, which happens when the encoder turns too fast for the sample rate. Accumulators collect results so the application need not read every sample. Optional debounce filters and an LED drive output for optical encoders are included.

To change SAMPLEPER, stop the decoder with STOP, change it after STOPPED, then START again; otherwise behaviour is unpredictable. LEDPOL, REPORTPER, DBFEN and LEDPRE are also best changed only while stopped.

The LED output follows the sample period: it turns on LEDPRE before each sample and off right after. LEDPOL sets its polarity. For mechanical encoders without an LED, PSEL.LED set to Disconnected frees the pin.

Each phase input has a digital debounce filter (DBFEN). When on, the inputs are sampled at 1 MHz through the whole sample period and a level passes only if every sample in the period agrees: a level steady for more than twice SAMPLEPER always passes, one steady for less than SAMPLEPER never does. The input is assumed to stay below 500 kHz during debouncing. With the filters on, the LED stays on (sampling is continuous) and reported movement lags by one SAMPLEPER.

ACC sums the valid ±1 samples, giving the movement since it was last cleared; double transitions (2) are not added to it. A sample that would overflow or underflow ACC is dropped and gives ACCOF, while later samples that fit are still taken. ACCDBL counts double transitions. READCLRACC copies both to ACCREAD and ACCDBLREAD and clears them; RDCLRACC does so for ACC alone and RDCLRDBL for ACCDBL alone. REPORTPER sets how many samples are gathered before evaluation: then REPORTRDY fires if the movement is non-zero, and DBLRDY if any double transition was counted. RDCLRACC and RDCLRDBL can be triggered by hand on those events or by the DBLRDY_RDCLRACC and DBLRDY_RDCLRDBL shortcuts.

The decoder uses three pins, A, B and LED, chosen by PSEL.A, PSEL.B and PSEL.LED and taken when ENABLE is set; while taken the CPU can read but not write them. CONNECT=Disconnected leaves a signal unconnected. The settings apply only while enabled and are kept only in System ON; when disabled the pins act as ordinary GPIO. The pins should be set in GPIO before enabling and kept so while enabled. Only one peripheral may drive a given pin.

The QSPI interface (base 0x40029000) talks to external flash in single, dual or quad SPI at a clock of 2 to 32 MHz. It offers single-word access, EasyDMA block reads and writes (up to 16 MB/s read), and execute in place (XIP) so the CPU runs code straight from the flash. Signals are SCK, CSN and IO0 to IO3.

Before any transfer: choose the pins in PSEL.SCK, PSEL.CSN and PSEL.IO0 to IO3 (the reference circuits give recommended pins); set those GPIOs to high drive for stable operation; set the flash interface in IFCONFIG0, IFCONFIG1 and ADDRCONF; set ENABLE to take the pins; trigger ACTIVATE, after which READY means the interface and flash are ready. If IFCONFIG0 selects quad mode, the flash itself must also be put in quad mode first, by a custom instruction.

A write is set by WRITE.DST, WRITE.SRC and WRITE.CNT and started by WRITESTART; a read by READ.SRC, READ.DST and READ.CNT and started by READSTART. READY marks completion, and writes are split into page programs automatically. An erase is set by ERASE.PTR and ERASE.LEN and started by ERASESTART; READY then only says the erase has begun, and its progress is checked by querying the flash with a custom instruction.
Once configured, code in the external flash runs by reading the XIP region of the memory map, whose start maps to flash address XIPOFFSET. The region is read-only; writing to it gives a bus error.

A custom instruction is a one-byte opcode with up to 8 data bytes, always sent on a single data line, and its reply can be read. Load the data in CINSTRDAT0 and CINSTRDAT1, then write the opcode and settings to CINSTRCONF, which sends it; READY follows and the two data registers then hold the reply. Long frame mode (LFEN and LFSTOP in CINSTRCONF) allows instructions of any length: every write to CINSTRCONF has LFEN = 1, the opcode goes out only on the first write, each later write sends LENGTH − 1 data bytes, LIO2 and LIO3 are fixed by the first write for the whole frame, and LFSTOP = 1 on the last write ends it.

The flash can be put in deep power-down to cut its current when not needed. IFCONFIG0 enables it, DPMDUR sets its timing (to match the flash so STATUS and READY timing are right), IFCONFIG1 enters and leaves it, and STATUS reports it.
IFTIMING.RXDELAY (reset 2) sets how many 64 MHz cycles, 15.625 ns each, pass after the rising SCK edge before input data is sampled; 0 samples on the rising edge itself.

The 2.4 GHz transceiver (base 0x40001000) supports Bluetooth LE at 1 and 2 Mbps plus the 125 kbps and 500 kbps long-range rates, IEEE 802.15.4 at 250 kbps, and Nordic proprietary 1 Mbps and 2 Mbps modes. EasyDMA with hardware packet assembly and disassembly and CRC generation and checking moves packets to and from RAM. It also has automatic address filtering and pattern matching, units for device address matching and interframe spacing in Bluetooth LE whitelisting and timing, an RSSI and a bit counter that raises events after a set number of bits.

On air a packet is PREAMBLE, ADDRESS (base address then prefix), S0, LENGTH, S1, PAYLOAD, an optional static add-on (PCNF1.STATLEN, 0 bytes in standard BLE) and CRC; in BLE long range CI, TERM1 and TERM2 fields follow the address and the payload. The preamble goes LSB first; it is one byte in Ble_1Mbit and the Nordic modes and two bytes in Ble_2Mbit (PCNF0.PLEN set to match), 0xAA or 0xAAAA if the first address bit is 0 and 0x55 or 0x5555 otherwise; 10 repeats of 0x3C in Ble_LR125Kbit and Ble_LR500Kbit; and four zero bytes in Ieee802154_250Kbit. In RAM a packet holds only S0, LENGTH, S1 and PAYLOAD. ADDRESS and PAYLOAD go least significant byte first, CRC most significant byte first; address bits go LSB first, CRC bits MSB first, and PCNF1.ENDIAN sets the bit order of S0, LENGTH, S1 and PAYLOAD. S0LEN, LFLEN and S1LEN in PCNF0 size those fields; a field shorter than 8 bits uses the low bits, a zero-length field is absent in RAM, and any other takes whole bytes. S0, LENGTH, S1 and PAYLOAD together cannot exceed 258 bytes, whatever MAXLEN says.

The on-air address is a base address, whose length PCNF1.BALEN sets (cut from the least significant byte when BALEN is under 4), plus a prefix byte. The BASEn and PREFIXn registers hold the on-air values; TXADDRESS, RXADDRESSES and RXMATCH use logical addresses 0 to 7.

With PCNF1.WHITEEN set, packets are whitened and de-whitened automatically over everything except preamble and address. The whitening sequence comes from a 7-bit LFSR with polynomial D7 + D4 + 1, XORed with the data; DATAWHITEIV sets its start value.

The CRC covers the whole packet except the preamble, and optionally excludes the address too (CRCCNF). Its length n and its polynomial (CRCPOLY, bit k standing for X^k) are configurable, and CRCINIT preloads the generator. The computed CRC cannot be read by the CPU, but the received CRC can be read from RXCRC whether or not it passed. After reception CRCOK or CRCERROR fires and CRCSTATUS holds the result.

Tasks and events drive the states: TXEN or RXEN starts ramp-up and READY marks TXIDLE or RXIDLE; START begins the packet, giving ADDRESS, PAYLOAD (always, even for a zero-length payload), END and, on transmit, PHYEND at the last bit; STOP returns to idle; DISABLE leads through TXDISABLE or RXDISABLE to DISABLED. The radio does not block a task given in the wrong state, which can cause wrong behaviour. In Ble_LR125Kbit, Ble_LR500Kbit and Ieee802154_250Kbit the PHYEND to START shortcut should be used rather than END to START.

START can be given only after READY. Without shortcuts, CPU latency separates READY from START and END from DISABLE; during those gaps the transmitter sends ones by default (MODECNF0.DTX changes this), and the receiver listens and may pick up undefined data until a valid preamble arrives. The READY_START and END_DISABLE shortcuts remove those delays. Several packets can be sent or received back to back without disabling in between.

The received signal strength is measured continuously through a single-pole IIR filter and settles within about RSSISETTLE of a level change. RSSISTART takes a sample, readable in RSSISAMPLE after RSSIPERIOD. A sample is valid only with the receiver enabled (RXEN) and reception started (READY then START).

TIFS sets the time from the last bit of a received packet to the first bit of the next transmitted one, and the radio enforces it provided it is not below the turnaround time. It is enforced only with END_DISABLE plus DISABLED_TXEN or DISABLED_RXEN shortcuts, and is qualified in BLE 1 Mbit, 2 Mbit, LR125 kbit, LR500 kbit and IEEE 802.15.4 modes with the default ramp-up. TIFS and SHORTS are not double-buffered and may change any time before the last bit is received; MODE is double-buffered and sampled at TXEN or RXEN.

For Bluetooth LE whitelisting the radio can compare up to eight device addresses on the fly while receiving, in little-endian configuration only. It treats the first 48 payload bits as the device address and bit 6 of S0 as TxAdd. Each address is a DAB (low 32 bits) and DAP (high 16 bits) pair with a TxAdd bit in DACNF, where each can be enabled or not. DEVMATCH or DEVMISS reports the result.

BCSTART starts a bit counter, allowed only after the ADDRESS event, and BCMATCH fires when it reaches BCC; it keeps counting until DISABLED or BCSTOP, so BCC can be raised for further matches in the same packet. BCSTOP, STOP, END and DISABLE stop and reset it. Shortcuts can start it from radio events.

MODE=Ieee802154_250Kbit gives the IEEE 802.15.4-2006 250 kbps O-QPSK PHY at 2450 MHz, with clear channel assessment, energy detection scans and CRC generation. A frame is a synchronisation header (four zero preamble bytes and an SFD of 0xA7, both made by the radio; SFD can change it for non-standard filtering), a PHR length byte (7-bit length, the top bit reserved but reported), and a PSDU of up to 127 bytes, 125 usable when the 2-byte CRC is used. Timing: SHR 160 µs, PHR 32 µs, PSDU up to 4064 µs; a symbol is 16 µs. PHR is the first byte stored at PACKETPTR; zero-length frames are discarded without FRAMESTART. The MAC frame within is FCF (2 bytes), sequence number, addressing fields (0 to 20 bytes), payload and a 16-bit FCS (ITU-T CRC over header and payload).

Energy detection averages RSSI over 8 symbols (128 µs) with the receiver on and the READY to START shortcut off, so nothing is decoded. EDSTART begins it and EDEND ends it with the level in EDSAMPLE; EDSTOP aborts, followed by EDSTOPPED. The IEEE scale (0 to 0xFF) is the hardware value times ED_RSSISCALE, saturating at 255 for values over 63. With EDCNT non-zero, the measurement repeats that many extra times (total 128 × N µs for EDCNT = N − 1) and reports the maximum, cutting interrupts and power during channel scans.

CCA needs the receiver on and able to receive, with the READY to START shortcut off if no packet processing is wanted, and surveys 8 symbols (128 µs). CCACTRL.CCAMODE: EdMode reports busy when the measured energy is at or above CCAEDTHRES; CarrierMode reports busy when a valid SFD is seen, or a frame is being received, or (with CCACORRCNT non-zero) the correlator output exceeds CCACORRTHRES more than CCACORRCNT times; CarrierAndEdMode and CarrierOrEdMode combine the two with AND or OR; EdModeTest1 aborts at the first measurement over threshold without averaging. CCASTART begins it, CCABUSY or CCAIDLE ends it, and CCASTOP aborts it with CCASTOPPED. Shortcuts: CCAIDLE to TXEN, always used together with CCAIDLE to STOP, to switch straight to transmit; CCABUSY to DISABLE; and RXREADY to CCASTART to begin CCA once the receiver is up.

The 16-bit ITU-T CRC covers the MAC header and payload. On receive it starts with the first byte after PHR, CRCSTATUS updates at frame end and CRCOK or CRCERROR fires, and the two CRC bytes are not written to RAM. On transmit EasyDMA fetches length − 2 bytes and the radio appends the CRC computed on the fly; the FCS is little-endian.

Transmission starts in receive: RXEN, then on READY a CCA (CCASTART); 128 µs later CCAIDLE or CCABUSY.
