On CCABUSY the CCA is retried after the standard's back-off; on CCAIDLE, TXEN ramps to TXIDLE and READY, then START with PACKETPTR at the PHR sends preamble, SFD, PHR and the frame. CRC settings are sampled at START. Shortcuts READY to CCASTART and CCAIDLE to TXEN automate the sequence.

RXEN, READY, then START enables processing. After a valid SHR, bytes from PHR on are stored at PACKETPTR and FRAMESTART fires after the SFD. CRCOK fires if the CRC over the full frame comes to zero, and END when the last byte is in RAM. A link quality indicator follows the last stored byte (after the MSDU for a compliant frame, since the FCS is not stored); it comes from the median of three RSSI readings during the frame, is valid for frames of three bytes or more, and is scaled to the IEEE range by a saturating multiply by 4. A FRAMESTART to BCSTART shortcut lets the bit counter flag a point such as the addressing fields.

Frames must be separated by the IFS: 12 symbols (macMinSIFSPeriod) after an MPDU of up to 18 bytes (aMaxSIFSFrameSize), and 40 symbols (macMinLIFSPeriod) after a longer one; an acknowledgement follows its frame after 32 symbols (tack). The assisted modes set TIFS automatically; otherwise software must update it.

One pointer, PACKETPTR, serves receive and transmit; it is double-buffered and should be set before each START. Outside Data RAM a transfer can cause a HardFault or RAM corruption. END marks the last bit processed and DISABLED the completion of DISABLE. RAM holds S0, LENGTH, S1 and PAYLOAD, each padded to whole bytes (3 bits take 1 byte, 9 bits take 2), with the static add-on after the payload; any field may be zero length. PCNF1.MAXLEN caps payload plus add-on in bytes, excluding S0, LENGTH and S1. A longer packet is still sent or received but with the payload cut at MAXLEN, the LENGTH field left as is, and the CRC computed as if the length were MAXLEN.
The POWER register (offset 0xFFC, reset 1) switches the radio peripheral off and on; doing so returns it and its registers to their reset state.

The random number generator (base 0x4000D000) produces true, non-deterministic random numbers from internal thermal noise, fit for cryptographic use, and needs no seed. START runs it and STOP halts it; while running it keeps writing new bytes to VALUE, each announced by VALRDY, and a byte must be read before the next VALRDY overwrites it.

An optional bias correction (CONFIG.DERCEN) removes any lean towards 1 or 0 in the bit stream, giving a statistically uniform result at a slower rate; bits are gathered eight at a time into VALUE. The time per byte cannot be predicted and varies from byte to byte, more so with bias correction on.

The real-time counter is a low-power timer clocked from LFCLK, with a 24-bit COUNTER, a 12-bit prescaler, capture/compare registers CC[0..N] with COMPARE events, an OVRFLW event and a TICK event for tickless RTOS scheduling. Tasks are START, STOP, CLEAR and TRIGOVRFLW.
The RTC runs on LFCLK, which software must start first; the counter resolution at 32.768 kHz is 30.517 µs. Depending on the LFCLK source it can keep running with HFCLK off and PCLK16M absent.

PRESCALER can be written only while the RTC is stopped; once started it reads back but writes have no effect. Its value is latched into the internal prescaler on START, CLEAR and TRIGOVRFLW. The counter steps when the internal prescaler count reaches 0, after which it reloads.

OVRFLW comes when COUNTER wraps from 0xFFFFFF to 0; TRIGOVRFLW sets COUNTER to 0xFFFFF0 to test this. TICK, if enabled, comes on every counter step and gives an RTOS a regular interrupt without SysTick, so the CPU can power down while scheduling continues. Both events are off by default.

EVTEN enables events one by one; a disabled event does not request PCLK16M and HFCLK, which saves power. A frequent event such as TICK should be disabled when not needed so HFCLK can stay off. Each event reaches the PPI when enabled in EVTEN and the NVIC when enabled in INTEN.

COMPARE fires when the counter steps from N−1 to N with CC = N. No COMPARE comes from CC = 0 at a CLEAR, nor from CC = N when START is given with the counter already at N. With the counter at N, writing N+2 to CC is sure to fire at N+2, while N or N+1 may not fire. If CC held N+1 or N+2 when a new value is written, the old value may still match first; if it held more than N+2, it will not.

LFCLK is not synchronous with PCLK16M, so registers seen by the CPU mirror registers in the LFCLK domain and must cross between them, which adds delay and jitter. CLEAR, STOP and TRIGOVRFLW wait for an LFCLK falling and rising edge, 15.2585 µs to 45.7755 µs (taken as 15 µs and 46 µs). With LFCLK already stable, the first counter step (and TICK) after START comes typically 30.5 µs ± 15 µs later, but up to about 250 µs if the RTC is started before LFCLK runs; waiting for the first TICK confirms the RTC is running. TRIGOVRFLW with LFCLK stopped starts LFCLK and is delayed likewise.
Reading COUNTER samples the internal counter safely by holding the CPU and bus for three cycles (PREADY low); with the two cycles of the read itself, a COUNTER read always takes five PCLK16M cycles.

The SAADC is a differential successive-approximation ADC with 8, 10 or 12-bit resolution, and 14 bits by oversampling. It has up to eight single-ended or four differential channels (the count depends on the package). Its inputs are the pins AIN0 to AIN7 plus VDD and VDDHDIV5 (VDDH divided by five). Each channel picks its own reference, VDD or the internal reference, and the full-scale range runs from 0 V to VDD. Sampling can run continuously, and EasyDMA writes every result to RAM as a 16-bit two's complement word. An internal resistor ladder can bias each input.

Writing CH[n].PSELP picks the positive input of channel n and enables it; CH[n].PSELN picks the negative input and matters only in differential mode. CH[n].CONFIG holds the channel's mode, reference, gain, acquisition time and ladder setting. In single-ended mode the negative side is tied to the ADC's internal ground, which is then assumed equal to the ground the signal is measured against, so board ground bounce shows up in the result; differential mode avoids that.

RESULT.PTR (buffer address) and RESULT.MAXCNT (buffer length) are set before sampling, and the START task applies the configuration. STOP ends sampling and aborts any conversion under way; the STOPPED event follows, and it comes even when the SAADC was not running.
The SAADC shares analog circuits with the other analog peripherals. COMP and SAADC may run at the same time but must not use the same analog input pin.

To take a sample the SAADC switches a sampling capacitor onto the input for the acquisition time TACQ, set per channel in CH[n].CONFIG. A source with higher resistance needs a longer TACQ, as the acquisition-time table gives. With VDDHDIV5 as the input, TACQ is 10 µs or more.

Each of the positive and negative inputs has an internal resistor string that can pull the input up or down through a resistor R. RESP sets it for the positive input and RESN for the negative input, both in CH[n].CONFIG. The ladder resistance is 160 kΩ typical.

Every channel has its own reference, VDD/4 or the internal 0.6 V, and its own gain from 1/6 to 4; together they set the input range. With the VDD reference, a single-ended input and gain 1/4, the range is 0 to VDD; with the internal reference and gain 1/6 it is 3.6 V. AIN0 to AIN7 must stay between VSS and VDD.

Three modes exist and only one runs at a time. One channel enabled gives single conversion or continuous conversion; two or more enabled channels put the SAADC in scan mode. Oversampling raises the signal-to-noise ratio and is not recommended in scan mode.

With one channel enabled, each SAMPLE task takes one conversion and the SAADC then stops. DONE marks the sample; without oversampling RESULTDONE comes with it, and both can arrive before EasyDMA has written the value. END comes once RESULT.MAXCNT results are in RAM.

One channel is sampled over and over, paced by the SAADC's own timer, which SAMPLERATE enables and sets. A single SAMPLE task starts it and STOP ends it. DONE comes per sample (with RESULTDONE when not oversampling), and END once RESULT.MAXCNT results are written. The sample rate must be below 1/(tACQ + tCONV).

With more than one channel enabled, one SAMPLE task converts every enabled channel once. A channel takes tACQ + tCONV; sampling all of them takes less than the sum over the enabled channels. DONE and RESULTDONE mark each sample and may come before the RAM write. Continuous conversion cannot be used in scan mode.

An accumulator averages 2^OVERSAMPLE input samples (OVERSAMPLE register) into each result written to RAM. This improves the signal-to-noise ratio but not INL or DNL. DONE comes for every input sample, RESULTDONE for every averaged result, and END after RESULT.MAXCNT averaged results. Because the average runs across all enabled channels, oversampling is meant for one enabled channel only.

Each result is sign-extended to 16 bits and written little-endian. DC errors (offset, gain, DNL and INL) move the result, and these weigh most in battery measurement; AC errors come from non-linearity in the gain stage, incomplete settling with a high source impedance, and sampling jitter.

EasyDMA writes results to the buffer at RESULT.PTR; RESULT.MAXCNT is its length in 16-bit samples, and both are set before START. RESULT.PTR is double-buffered: after STARTED it may be loaded with the next buffer's address. END comes when the buffer is full. Results fill RAM two to a 32-bit word, low half first, in the order of the enabled channels' numbers and then round again; with an odd RESULT.MAXCNT the last word holds a single result. EasyDMA has finished with RAM at END or STOPPED, and RESULT.AMOUNT counts the results written since START.

CH[n].LIMIT sets a high and a low limit per channel, the high one not below the low one. A result above the high limit raises LIMITH and one below the low limit raises LIMITL; swapping the limits does not give an event for a signal inside a band. Limit checking needs no enabling, and the events can simply be ignored when not wanted.

The SAADC's offset drifts with temperature. It should be calibrated at least once before use and again whenever the ambient temperature moves by more than 10 °C. The CALIBRATEOFFSET task starts offset calibration and CALIBRATEDONE marks its end.

SPI is the older SPI master without EasyDMA, kept for legacy use. The CPU writes bytes to TXD and reads them from RXD; both are double-buffered so data can keep flowing. It has no chip-select output, so software drives a GPIO to select each slave. SPI modes 0 to 3 are supported.

PSEL.SCK, PSEL.MOSI and PSEL.MISO map the signals to pins; a PSEL set to Disconnected leaves its signal off every pin. They take effect only while SPI is enabled, are kept only in System ON, and are written only while SPI is disabled. The pins are set up in GPIO as the SPI GPIO table lists before SPI is enabled, and kept that way while it runs. SCK must be on a pin whose input buffer is connected. A pin is driven by one peripheral at a time.

SPI shares its registers with the other peripherals of the same ID, which are disabled before SPI is set up. Disabling one of them does not reset the shared registers, so every SPI register in use is written explicitly.

Writing the first byte to TXD starts a transfer, and the second may follow at once; bytes go out in the order written. Each byte sent clocks one byte in, which moves into RXD (itself double-buffered) a short time after the byte's last SCK period, raising READY. A byte waiting in RXD-1 moves into RXD only after RXD is read, so the READY for that byte waits for the read. The transfer stops when TXD and its buffer are empty. READY is always cleared, even when the received data is not used.

SPIM is the SPI master with EasyDMA. It talks to several slaves, each on its own chip select, moves data straight between RAM and the bus, supports SPI modes 0 to 3, lets every signal use any pin, and can drive an optional D/CX line that tells command bytes from data bytes.

The START task begins a transfer. ENDTX comes when all TXD.MAXCNT bytes of the TXD.PTR buffer are sent, ENDRX when RXD.MAXCNT bytes have filled the RXD.PTR buffer, and END once both have come; the transfer then stops by itself. If the receive count is larger, the ORC byte is sent after the transmit buffer runs out; if the transmit count is larger, the surplus received bytes are dropped. STOP lets the byte in progress finish and then gives STOPPED, which comes even with no transfer running; on such a stop ENDTX and ENDRX are still raised if they had not come. SUSPEND halts after the current byte and RESUME carries on.

Some slaves, display drivers for example, need a line telling command bytes from data bytes. SPIM drives D/CX low while command bytes go out and high for data bytes. PSELDCX picks its pin and DCXCNT sets how many command bytes lead the data; DCXCNT is not written during a transfer.

The PSEL registers map SCK, CSN, DCX, MOSI and MISO to pins. They take effect only while SPIM is enabled (ENABLE register), are kept only in System ON, and are written only while SPIM is disabled. The pins are set up in GPIO as the SPIM GPIO table lists before enabling, and a pin is driven by one peripheral at a time. Instances without hardware CSN control leave chip select to a GPIO. CONFIG sets CPOL and CPHA.

TXD reads RAM and RXD writes it. Both .PTR and .MAXCNT have a second buffer stage, so they may be loaded for the next transfer as soon as STARTED has come. ENDTX and ENDRX mark the end of RAM access for each buffer and END the end of both. How a channel copes when several AHB masters contend for one slave depends on the instance.
For the lowest current an idle SPIM is stopped and disabled. When STOP is sent, software waits for STOPPED before clearing ENABLE.

On instances that drive CSN, CSNPOL sets whether CSN is active low (0) or active high (1), and IFTIMING.CSNDUR sets the time between CSN going active and the first SCK edge, and between the last SCK edge and CSN going inactive.

SPIS is an SPI slave with EasyDMA. A hardware semaphore over its buffers means it can be serviced from low-priority code with no real-time demands on the CPU. CONFIG sets CPOL and CPHA for SPI modes 0 to 3.
SPIS shares its registers with the other peripherals of the same ID, which are disabled first. Disabling them does not reset the shared registers, so every SPIS register in use is written explicitly.
TXD reads RAM and RXD writes it. When RXD.MAXCNT exceeds TXD.MAXCNT, the bytes sent after the transmit buffer is used up carry the ORC value. END marks the end of EasyDMA's access to the buffer.

RXD.PTR and TXD.PTR point at the receive and transmit buffers in RAM, which the CPU and SPIS share under a hardware semaphore. The CPU takes it with the ACQUIRE task and holds it once ACQUIRED comes; after updating the pointers it hands it back with RELEASE (RELEASE without holding it does nothing). The semaphore only signals when updates are safe and never blocks CPU access. After SPIS is enabled the CPU holds it, with no ACQUIRED event; ACQUIRE while the CPU already holds it gives ACQUIRED at once. SPIS tries to take the semaphore when CSN falls. If it cannot, the transaction is ignored: MOSI data is thrown away and the DEF byte goes out on MISO for the whole transaction, even if the CPU releases partway. If both ask at the same moment, the CPU wins. In a granted transaction MOSI fills the RXD buffer and the TXD buffer goes out on MISO; when CSN rises SPIS releases the semaphore and raises END.

While the semaphore is free, SPIS can be granted one transaction after another; if the CPU does not move the pointers in between, the same transmit data repeats and received data overwrites the last. The END_ACQUIRE shortcut gives the semaphore to the CPU after each granted transaction so it can update them every time. An ACQUIRE during a granted transaction is served when that transaction ends, and with END_ACQUIRE on only one such request is served after END.

RXD.MAXCNT caps the bytes received in one granted transaction: more sets OVERFLOW in STATUS and the extra bytes are dropped. TXD.MAXCNT caps the bytes sent: more sets OVERREAD in STATUS and the ORC byte is clocked out. RXD.AMOUNT and TXD.AMOUNT are updated at the end of each granted transaction: RXD.AMOUNT counts bytes put in the receive buffer, TXD.AMOUNT bytes taken from the transmit buffer (ORC bytes not counted). ENDRX comes when the receive buffer is full.

Four PSEL registers (one each for CSN, SCK, MOSI, MISO) map the signals to pins (Disconnected leaves a signal off every pin). They take effect only while SPIS is enabled, are kept only in System ON, and are written only while it is disabled; a disabled SPIS leaves its pins as ordinary GPIOs following OUT and PIN_CNF[n]. Setting the pins up in GPIO as the SPIS table lists before enabling keeps them correct while SPIS is briefly disabled or the chip is in System OFF, and this is kept for as long as an external master should see the slave. MISO is high impedance while CSN is not asserted. A pin is driven by one peripheral at a time.
Six interrupts, SWI0 to SWI5, are set aside for software to trigger.

TEMP measures the die temperature over at least the device's operating range, with 0.25 °C steps; the application can add linearity correction. The START task begins a measurement, DATARDY marks its end, and the TEMP register then holds the result. The stated accuracy needs the crystal oscillator as the HFCLK source. The analog part powers down after each measurement, and every measurement is started on its own by START (one-shot only).

TWI is the older I2C-compatible master without EasyDMA, for 100 kHz and 400 kHz. It is not CBUS compatible, its transmitter and receiver hold one byte each, and it must be the only master on the bus. It honours clock stretching by slaves. STARTTX or STARTRX starts it, STOP stops it, and a NACK from the slave raises ERROR.

PSEL.SCL and PSEL.SDA map the signals to pins (Disconnected leaves a signal off every pin). They take effect only while TWI is enabled, are kept only in System ON, and are written only while TWI is disabled. Setting the pins up in GPIO as the TWI table lists keeps their levels right in System OFF and while TWI is disabled. A pin is driven by one peripheral at a time.
TWI shares its registers with the other peripherals of the same ID, which are disabled first; disabling them does not reset the shared registers, so every TWI register in use is written.

STARTTX sends a start condition, the address and the R/W bit at 0, and the slave answers ACK or NACK. The bytes written to TXD then go out, each followed by the slave's ACK/NACK, and TXDSENT comes after each one. TXD takes the next byte only after TXDSENT; if the CPU is late, the master stretches the clock until it writes. STOP ends the write with a stop condition.

STARTRX sends a start condition, the address and the R/W bit at 1; after its ACK the slave sends data on the master's clock. RXDRDY comes for every byte in RXD, and the master holds the ACK/NACK bit, stretching the clock, until the CPU reads RXD. STOP is triggered before the last byte is read so that the master answers it with NACK and then sends the stop condition.

Write and read sequences chain without a stop between them, for example one byte written and then M bytes read. Only one shortcut to STOP may be enabled at a time. After a read, a repeated start is made by triggering STARTRX or STARTTX instead of STOP, before the last byte is read, so the NACK goes out first.
For the lowest current an idle TWI is stopped and then disabled; if STOP is sent, software waits for STOPPED before clearing ENABLE.

TIMER is a general-purpose timer/counter clocked from HFCLK through a four-bit prescaler that divides by a power of two. The base frequency is always 16 MHz divided by the prescaler value, and the source, PCLK16M or PCLK1M, is chosen automatically from it: at fTIMER of 1 MHz or less TIMER runs on PCLK1M to save current. Through the PPI a TIMER event can trigger any other peripheral's task, and with GPIOTE it can make periodic outputs and PWM on any GPIO, as many at once as there are GPIOTE channels.

In both modes START runs the timer and STOP halts it; a later START continues from the value it held. In Timer mode the counter steps once per fTIMER tick. In Counter mode it steps once per COUNT task and the prescaler is unused; COUNT does nothing in Timer mode. BITMODE sets the counter's bit width and so its maximum; PRESCALER and BITMODE are changed only while the timer is stopped, or the behaviour is unpredictable. Past its maximum the counter wraps to zero, and CLEAR sets it to zero. Whatever the prescaler, the timer is accurate to one fTIMER tick.

Each capture/compare register CC[n] has a CAPTURE[n] task, which copies the counter into CC[n], and a COMPARE[n] event, raised when the counter steps to a value equal to CC[n]. Only the bits BITMODE selects take part in the comparison.
Once the timer is running, CLEAR, COUNT and STOP take effect within one PCLK16M cycle. When START and STOP arrive in the same PCLK16M period, STOP wins.

TWIM is an I2C-compatible two-wire master with EasyDMA, half duplex, at 100, 250 or 400 kbps. It supports clock stretching (not I2C compliant), addresses up to 127 devices on the wired-AND SCL/SDA bus, and is not CBUS compatible. SCL and SDA can each be any GPIO. It must be the only master on the bus.

TWIM honours clock stretching by slaves, though the SCL pulse after a stretched cycle may be shorter than I2C allows. STARTTX or STARTRX starts it; STOP stops it and STOPPED follows. Once started, STARTTX and STARTRX are not triggered again until LASTRX, LASTTX or STOPPED has come. SUSPEND, useful when TWIM is served from a low-priority interrupt, lets the current byte finish and then holds SCL low, raising SUSPENDED, until RESUME; it does nothing unless a transfer is running. TWIM cannot be stopped while suspended, so it is resumed before STOP. A NACK from the slave raises ERROR.

TXD reads RAM and RXD writes it. Both .PTR and .MAXCNT have a second buffer stage and can be loaded for the next transfer once RXSTARTED or TXSTARTED has come. STOPPED marks the end of EasyDMA's access to RAM.

STARTTX sends a start condition, the address and the R/W bit at 0; after the slave's ACK the bytes of the TXD.PTR buffer go out, each followed by the slave's ACK/NACK. SUSPENDED shows a SUSPEND has taken hold. LASTTX comes as the last byte starts. STOP is triggered during that last byte, or by the LASTTX to STOP shortcut, so the bus is released quickly. TWIM does not stop by itself at the end of the buffer or on an error: STOP must come from a shortcut, the PPI or the error handler.

STARTRX sends a start condition, the address and the R/W bit at 1; the slave then sends data on the master's clock into the RXD.PTR buffer. TWIM ACKs every byte except the last, which it NACKs. LASTRX comes when the last byte is about to be received: after the ACK of the byte before when RXD.MAXCNT is above 1, or after the address ACK when it is 1. STOP must be triggered before the NACK is due, at any point during the last byte; the LASTRX to STOP shortcut is the recommended way. TWIM does not stop by itself when the buffer fills or on an error, and it is resumed before a STOP if suspended.

A write followed by a read with a repeated start between them (for example two bytes written, four read) can run on shortcuts alone: LASTTX starts the read and LASTRX triggers STOP. A read followed by a write works the same way. For longer chains driven from a low-priority interrupt, SUSPEND and SUSPENDED keep each task in its place, as in a double repeated start.
For the lowest current an idle TWIM is stopped and then disabled; after STOP, software waits for STOPPED before clearing ENABLE. If TWIM is already stopped, STOP is not needed.

PSEL.SCL and PSEL.SDA map the signals to pins. They take effect only while TWIM is enabled, are kept only in System ON, and are written only while it is disabled; a disabled TWIM leaves the pins as GPIOs following OUT and PIN_CNF[n]. The GPIO setup in the TWIM table keeps the levels right in System OFF and while TWIM is disabled. A pin is driven by one peripheral at a time.

The recommended pull-up falls as line capacitance rises: at 100 kbps about 24 kΩ at 50 pF, 12 kΩ at 100 pF, 6 kΩ at 200 pF and 5 kΩ at 400 pF; at 400 kbps about 7 kΩ at 50 pF, 3.5 kΩ at 100 pF, 1.7 kΩ at 200 pF and 1 kΩ at 400 pF. I2C allows at most 400 pF of line capacitance. The internal pull-up value RPU is given with the GPIO specification.
TWIS is an I2C-compatible two-wire slave for 100 kHz and 400 kHz, with EasyDMA in both directions. It works with a single master on the bus.

After ENABLE the slave is in IDLE. PREPARETX and PREPARERX set internal 'TX prepared' and 'RX prepared' flags. A read command with TX prepared moves it to TX, raising TXSTARTED and clearing the TX flag; a write command with RX prepared moves it to RX, raising RXSTARTED and clearing the RX flag. A restart condition sends it back to IDLE. A stop condition or the STOP task raises STOPPED, clears both flags and returns it to IDLE.

TWIS can stretch the clock when the master supports it, and stays in a low-power mode until a master addresses it. PSEL.SCL, PSEL.SDA, CONFIG and ADDRESS[n] are set before TWIS is enabled and changed only while it is disabled, or the behaviour is unpredictable.

A read command is a start condition, an address and the R/W bit at 1. TWIS listens for up to two addresses (ADDRESS registers and CONFIG), ACKs only a match, raises READ when it does, and sees read commands only from IDLE. With TX prepared it enters TX at once; otherwise it stretches the clock until PREPARETX. In TX it sends the TXD.PTR buffer on the master's clock, at most TXD.MAXCNT bytes per transaction; bytes asked for beyond that are the ORC value and raise ERROR. The EasyDMA registers are latched at TXSTARTED. The master NACKs the last byte it wants and then sends the stop condition; STOPPED follows, and TXD.AMOUNT gives the bytes sent. The STOP task forces a stop with the same result.

A write command is a start condition, an address and the R/W bit at 0. TWIS ACKs a matching address, raises WRITE, and sees write commands only from IDLE. With RX prepared it enters RX; otherwise it stretches the clock until PREPARERX. Received bytes go to the RXD.PTR buffer, at most RXD.MAXCNT of them; further bytes are NACKed, dropped, and raise ERROR. Every accepted byte is ACKed. The EasyDMA registers are latched at RXSTARTED. A stop condition or the STOP task ends it with STOPPED, and RXD.AMOUNT gives the bytes received.

When the bytes the master writes decide what it reads back, as in two bytes written and four read with a repeated start, the READ to SUSPEND shortcut holds the bus once the read command arrives. The CPU handles the received bytes, prepares the reply (TXD.PTR, TXD.MAXCNT, PREPARETX) and then triggers RESUME.
If the master misbehaves, the STOP task ends the transaction: STOPPED comes whether or not a stop condition appeared on the bus, and TWIS releases the bus and returns to IDLE.
For the lowest current an idle TWIS is stopped and then disabled; if STOP is sent, software waits for STOPPED before clearing ENABLE.

PSEL.SCL and PSEL.SDA map the signals to pins. They take effect only while TWIS is enabled, are kept only in System ON, and are written only while it is disabled; a disabled TWIS leaves the pins as GPIOs following OUT and PIN_CNF[n]. The GPIO setup in the TWIS table keeps the levels right in System OFF and while TWIS is disabled. A pin is driven by one peripheral at a time.

UART is the older UART without EasyDMA: full duplex, with automatic hardware flow control and parity generation and checking for a ninth data bit. It sends and receives through the TXD and RXD registers and uses one stop bit. The external crystal oscillator must run for the clock to be accurate enough for reliable communication.

The receive line RXD, the transmit line TXD, and the active-low handshake lines CTS (clear to send) and RTS (request to send) are mapped to pins by their PSEL registers; Disconnected leaves a signal off every pin. They take effect only while UART is enabled, are kept only in System ON, and are written only while it is disabled. The GPIO setup in the UART table keeps the pin levels right in System OFF. A pin is driven by one peripheral at a time.

UART shares its registers with the other peripherals of the same ID, which are disabled before it is set up; disabling them does not reset the shared registers, so every UART register in use is written explicitly.

STARTTX starts transmission. Each byte written to TXD is sent, and TXDRDY then says the next may be written. STOPTX stops transmission at once. With flow control on, transmission pauses when CTS goes inactive, after finishing the byte in progress, and continues when CTS is active again.

STARTRX starts reception. The receiver has a FIFO of six bytes, after which data is overwritten; reading RXD takes a byte and moves the next waiting one in, raising RXDRDY each time. With flow control on, RTS goes inactive when the FIFO has room for only four more bytes, so the sender must stop within four bytes; RTS goes active again only once the FIFO is empty. STOPRX also makes RTS inactive. Up to four or five more bytes sent straight after can still be received, for a time that depends on the baud rate, after which RXTO (receiver timeout) comes. RXD is read once per RXDRDY, and RXDRDY is cleared before RXD is read, since a new byte and event can follow the read at once.
SUSPEND halts both directions: the byte being sent is finished and the receiver acts as on STOPRX. STARTTX and STARTRX restart each side.
A frame without a valid stop bit raises ERROR as a framing error. RXD held low for longer than a frame raises ERROR as a break condition; a framing error always comes before the break.
With flow control off, the UART behaves as though CTS and RTS were held active.
CONFIG turns on even parity generation and checking in both directions and sets one or two stop bits.

UARTE is the UART with EasyDMA: full-duplex asynchronous serial up to 1 Mbps with hardware CTS/RTS flow control, optional even parity, one or two stop bits, LSB first, and a return to idle between transactions when hardware flow control is used. Each signal can be any GPIO. The external crystal oscillator must run for the clock to be accurate enough for reliable communication.

TXD.PTR and RXD.PTR must point into Data RAM; anything else can cause a HardFault or corrupt RAM. Both .PTR and .MAXCNT have a second buffer stage and may be loaded for the next transfer once RXSTARTED or TXSTARTED has come. ENDRX and ENDTX mark the end of EasyDMA's access to each buffer.

Software fills the transmit buffer, writes its address to TXD.PTR and its length to TXD.MAXCNT, and triggers STARTTX. TXDRDY comes after each byte; after TXD.MAXCNT bytes the transmission ends by itself with ENDTX. STOPTX stops it, TXSTOPPED follows, and ENDTX is raised then if it had not come. With flow control on (CONFIG.HWFC), sending pauses when CTS goes inactive, after the byte in progress, and continues when CTS is active. The transmitter draws least before STARTTX and after TXSTOPPED.

STARTRX starts the receiver, which stores data by EasyDMA in the buffer at RXD.PTR, RXD.MAXCNT bytes long. RXD.PTR is double-buffered and may be set for the next STARTRX once RXSTARTED has come. RXDRDY comes for each byte, usually before it reaches RAM, and ENDRX when the buffer is full; RXD.AMOUNT then gives the bytes written since the previous ENDRX. The ENDRX_STARTRX shortcut chains buffers for continuous reception.

STOPRX stops the receiver and RXTO follows. Any pending ENDRX comes before RXTO, and none comes after it unless the receiver is restarted or FLUSHRX is triggered; if the buffer was not full, ENDRX is raised anyway before RXTO. RXD.AMOUNT gives the byte count after ENDRX or RXTO. Up to four bytes sent straight after RTS goes inactive can still arrive, for the time four bytes take at the baud rate. Data left in the RX FIFO after RXTO is moved to RAM by FLUSHRX; the buffer is emptied or RXD.PTR moved first, and RXD.MAXCNT must be above 4 to take the whole FIFO. FLUSHRX always ends with ENDRX, even with an empty FIFO.

With hardware flow control on, RTS goes inactive on STOPRX or when the RX FIFO has room for only four more bytes. With it off the receiver works the same but RTS is unused, nothing warns the sender, and data arriving when the FIFO is full is lost; CTS and RTS are treated as always active. The receiver draws least before STARTRX and after RXTO.

A missing stop bit raises ERROR as a framing error; RXD held low longer than a frame raises ERROR as a break, always after a framing error. ERROR does not stop reception. A byte with a parity error is still written to RAM, as are those after it; a byte with a framing error is not, but the bytes after it are.

operation.topic: UARTE parity, stop bits and low power
operation.text: CONFIG sets even parity in both directions and one or two stop bits. For the lowest current an idle UARTE is stopped and disabled; after STOPTX or STOPRX, software waits for TXSTOPPED or RXTO before clearing ENABLE.

Each of RXD, TXD and the active-low CTS and RTS lines is mapped to a pin by its own PSEL register. They take effect only while UARTE is enabled, are kept only in System ON, and are written only while it is disabled. The GPIO setup in the UARTE table keeps the levels right in System OFF. A pin is driven by one peripheral at a time.

USBD is a full-speed (12 Mbps) USB 2.0 device controller, compliant including the Pull-up/pull-down Resistors ECN and the 5V Short Circuit Withstand Requirement Change ECN. It has an on-chip transceiver (PHY) powered from VBUS through its own regulator (DECUSB), a 48 MHz clock from a PLL on the HFXO, and a D+ pull-up under software control. Endpoints: two control (one IN, one OUT), fourteen bulk/interrupt (seven IN, seven OUT) and two isochronous (one IN, one OUT). Bulk/interrupt endpoints have 64-byte buffers; isochronous ones take up to 1023 bytes and are double-buffered. Suspend, resume and remote wake-up are supported, and all data moves by EasyDMA. A USB device stack is provided in the Nordic SDK.

The USB 2.0 chapter 9 states (attached, then powered, default, address and configured, each of these four with a suspended state) are tracked by software from host traffic and bus conditions. USBDETECTED and USBREMOVED report VBUS arriving and leaving. Software reacts to what the host actually does, never assuming a fixed enumeration order.
For a full-speed device, J is D+ high with D- low and K is the reverse. An idle bus, held only by the device's D+ pull-up and the host's pull-downs, sits in J. Both lines low is SE0, both high SE1.

D+ and D- are dedicated pins for the host connection, not usable as GPIO, and not 5 V tolerant (per the 5V Short Circuit Withstand ECN). They and the pull-up work only while VBUS is in its valid range and USBD is enabled in ENABLE.

The PHY runs from VBUS, and its supply is switched by ENABLE; the device cannot signal its presence or handle traffic until that supply is up and stable. The recommended order: wait for USBDETECTED (VBUS valid), write ENABLE, start the HFXO (HFCLKSTART), and turn on the pull-up (USBPULLUP) only after USBPWRRDY and a USBEVENT with READY in EVENTCAUSE have both come; HFCLKSTARTED marks the crystal running, and enumeration then begins. On USBREMOVED, ongoing EasyDMA transfers are allowed to finish (ENDEPIN[n], ENDISOIN, ENDEPOUT[n], ENDISOOUT) before USBD is disabled; ENABLE reads Enabled until USBD is fully off.

The host holds D+ and D- low through 15 kΩ resistors, so with no pull-up the device is detached and may draw no VBUS current. A full-speed device's 1.5 kΩ pull-up on D+ marks it attached and full speed; USBD supports full speed only and ignores the host's high-speed negotiation. USBPULLUP connects or removes the pull-up, so software decides when enumeration starts and can mimic an unplug for re-enumeration; it must be on for USBD to handle traffic, which rules out an external pull-up. Removing it while attached lets the host pull both lines low, and USBRESET is then not raised. It is off after chip reset and is turned on only after ENABLE. Its value changes with bus activity per the Resistor ECN, handled by hardware. The DPDMDRIVE task forces D+ and D- into the state in DPDMVALUE and DPDMNODRIVE returns the PHY to normal; this is not for normal traffic.

A USB reset is a bus condition, not a chip reset: SE0 held for longer than tUSB,DETRST, driven only by the host. USBD then raises USBRESET; the stack re-initialises and returns to the default state, all data endpoints are disabled and USBADDR goes to 0. From pull-up on until the first USB reset the device ignores traffic, which USBD ensures by itself. The device must be fully responsive within TRSTRCY (USB specification chapter 7) of a reset.

The host keeps the bus active at least every millisecond; to suspend the device it leaves the bus idle in J. After tUSB,SUSPEND without activity USBD raises USBEVENT with SUSPEND in EVENTCAUSE. Software then brings VBUS current within limits before T2SUSP and writes LowPower to LOWPOWER to cut USBD's idle current. The HFXO may be stopped during suspend, while the pull-up is off, or without VBUS, if nothing else needs it; at all other times it must run, as USBD answers traffic only with the HFXO running and stable.

When the host resumes (any non-J state) USBD raises USBEVENT with RESUME in EVENTCAUSE, and the device must answer within TRSMRCY; if the host simply restarts frames, SOF events follow. For remote wake-up, if the host has allowed it, software starts the HFXO, writes ForceNormal to LOWPOWER (a USBEVENT with USBWUALLOWED follows) and triggers DPDMDRIVE. With DPDMVALUE at Resume the K state lasts tUSB,DRIVEK under hardware timing; with J or K software holds it until DPDMNODRIVE and must meet TDRSMUP. DPDMVALUE is captured when DPDMDRIVE fires. No wake-up request may start before TWTRSM after the bus goes idle; the Resume value delays the K state to respect this.

EPINEN and EPOUTEN enable endpoints. EPIN[n].PTR and EPOUT[n].PTR (n = 0 to 7), ISOIN.PTR and ISOOUT.PTR hold buffer addresses. EPIN[n].MAXCNT and ISOIN.MAXCNT give the bytes to send in the next transaction; EPOUT[n].MAXCNT (n = 1 to 7) and ISOOUT.MAXCNT give the receive buffer length and can be copied from SIZE.EPOUT[n] or SIZE.ISOOUT, since the host decides the count. EPOUT[0].MAXCNT sets the control endpoint's OUT buffer, and SIZE.EPOUT[0] shows the smaller of MaxPacketSize and the SETUP wLength. The .AMOUNT registers give the bytes moved in the last transfer. EPSTALL stalls bulk/interrupt endpoints; a new SETUP can override a stall on endpoint 0. SETUP data is not moved by EasyDMA but read from BMREQUESTTYPE, BREQUEST, WVALUEL, WVALUEH, WINDEXL, WINDEXH, WLENGTHL and WLENGTHH. EVENTCAUSE says why a USBEVENT came (a CRC error, bus activity stopping or resuming).

STARTEPIN[n], STARTEPOUT[n] (n = 0 to 7), STARTISOIN and STARTISOOUT capture the .PTR and .MAXCNT values. An IN transaction follows automatically when its EasyDMA transfer ends; OUT transactions are allowed by software. On endpoint 0, EP0RCVOUT allows OUT transactions, EP0STATUS starts the status stage and EP0STALL stalls the data or status stage. STARTED says the registers of the endpoints flagged in EPSTATUS were captured and may be reloaded. ENDEPIN[n], ENDEPOUT[n], ENDISOIN and ENDISOOUT say a buffer is fully used and safe to touch. Only one EasyDMA transfer runs in USBD at a time, so no START task is triggered before the END event of the transfer in progress. EPDATA flags an acknowledged data transaction on the endpoints in EPDATASTATUS, EP0DATADONE does so for endpoint 0, EP0SETUP says SETUP data is in its registers, and USBEVENT can come at any time.

Endpoint 0 IN and OUT are the control endpoints, and their buffer may be any size. A control transfer has a setup stage, an optional data stage and a status stage, and is a control read or write, with or without data. After a SETUP, USBD NAKs IN and OUT tokens until software has decoded the request and prepared the next stage. An unsupported request, or one with a bad wValue, wIndex or wLength, is stalled with EP0STALL in the data or status stage. USBD handles SetAddress itself: software only updates its state, starts no status stage, and can read the new address from USBADDR.

Software points EPIN[0].PTR and EPIN[0].MAXCNT at the data and, with no other EasyDMA transfer running, triggers STARTEPIN0. STARTED (EPIN0 set in EPSTATUS) says the registers were captured, ENDEPIN[0] that the data reached USBD, and EP0DATADONE that the host acknowledged it. Software then sends the next packet the same way or starts the status stage with EP0STATUS; the EP0DATADONE to EP0STATUS shortcut suits a single-packet data stage. With no data stage, EP0STATUS is triggered straight away.

Software points EPOUT[0].PTR at the receive buffer and, with no other EasyDMA transfer running, triggers EP0RCVOUT so the first OUT+DATA is acknowledged. EP0DATADONE comes as each packet arrives; after STARTEPOUT[0], STARTED (EPOUT0 in EPSTATUS) and then ENDEPOUT[0] mark the data in memory. Software repeats for more packets or starts the status stage with EP0STATUS, and until then further OUT+DATA is NAKed. With no data stage, EP0STATUS is triggered straight away.

Seven pairs of bulk/interrupt endpoints have fixed numbers. Each transaction is a single data stage. USBD toggles DATA0/DATA1 itself and holds the toggle on a CRC error so the host resends; DTOGGLE forces the toggle on endpoint n (n = 1 to 7), for example after ClearFeature or SetInterface. A transaction is up to 64 bytes, and its buffer is a multiple of four bytes, 32-bit aligned. EPDATA comes when a transaction completes; IN tokens are NAKed until ENDEPIN[n] shows new data loaded. Endpoints are enabled in EPINEN and EPOUTEN to match the configuration the host selects; a disabled endpoint ignores the host, an enabled one answers NAK, ACK or STALL (EPSTALL). HALTED.EPIN[n] and HALTED.EPOUT[n] give a 16-bit value that can answer GetStatusEndpoint unchanged. Enabling or disabling does not change the halt state, but a USB reset disables all data endpoints and clears it. Endpoint 0 can be enabled and halted the same way, though a SETUP overrides it.

The host sends IN tokens; software enables the endpoint (INn bit in EPINEN) and starts an EasyDMA transfer on it. EPSTALL stalls or resumes it. A zero-length packet may be sent in answer to an IN token. Many hosts disable an interrupt endpoint that leaves three IN tokens unanswered, and re-enumeration may be needed to restore it, so endpoints are enabled as soon as SetConfig arrives.

The host sends an OUT token and a DATA packet to endpoint n (n = 1 to 7). USBD NAKs until software writes any value to SIZE.EPOUT[n], meaning the local buffer is free; the next OUT+DATA is then ACKed and EPDATA raised, with EPDATASTATUS showing the endpoint. Writing EPOUT[n] and triggering STARTEPOUT[n] moves the data to memory, and further OUT+DATA is NAKed until ENDEPOUT[n] or a new write to SIZE.EPOUT[n]. Zero-length packets are allowed. OUTn in EPOUTEN enables the endpoint and EPSTALL stalls it.

One isochronous IN and one OUT endpoint have fixed numbers. An isochronous transaction is one data stage with no acknowledge, following the start of frame the host sends every 1 ms. Software starts each EasyDMA transfer, in step with SOF events. SOF is synchronised to the 16 MHz clock before it reaches the PPI, so it can align a local timer. FRAMECNTR counts frames. The endpoints are enabled in EPINEN (ISOIN0) and EPOUTEN (ISOOUT0); a disabled one ignores the host. A 1 kB internal buffer serves both, split by ISOSPLIT: one direction alone takes up to 1023 bytes, and half that each when split. A transfer not finished before the next SOF gives an undefined result. The buffer in memory is a multiple of 4 bytes, 32-bit aligned, though the packet on the bus can be any size.

After the EasyDMA transfer, USBD answers the host's IN token with ISOIN.MAXCNT bytes. With the endpoint enabled and no data loaded, the RESPONSE field of ISOINCONFIG chooses between no answer and a zero-length packet.

SIZE.ISOOUT gives the size of the last OUT packet through its ZERO and SIZE fields. STARTISOOUT starts each EasyDMA transfer to memory using ISOOUT.PTR and ISOOUT.MAXCNT, in step with SOF. If the last packet had a bad CRC, USBEVENT comes with SOF and ISOOUTCRC set in EVENTCAUSE, and the data is still transferred if EasyDMA is set up.

While USBD is not enabled and ready (READY in EVENTCAUSE after a USBEVENT), or is in low-power mode during bus suspend, tasks (including those from the PPI) do not act, and these registers cannot be accessed: the setup data registers (BMREQUESTTYPE to WLENGTHH), USBADDR, USBPULLUP, FRAMECNTR, ISOSPLIT, DTOGGLE, SIZE.ISOOUT, SIZE.EPOUT[0..7], EPSTALL, EPOUTEN, EPINEN, HALTED.EPOUT[0..7] and HALTED.EPIN[0..7].

The watchdog is a down-counter on LFCLK that guards against the application locking up. START loads it from CRV and starts it; a granted reload loads CRV again. When it passes 0 it raises TIMEOUT. It can pause during long CPU sleep and while a debugger halts the CPU. Once started it keeps the 32.768 kHz RC oscillator on unless another 32.768 kHz source is already running.
Eight reload request registers RR[0] to RR[7] can be enabled one by one in RREN. Writing 0x6E524635 to every enabled RR register reloads the counter from CRV.
By default the watchdog keeps counting while the CPU sleeps and while the debugger halts it; it can be set to pause in either case.

TIMEOUT always causes a watchdog reset. With the TIMEOUT interrupt enabled, the reset comes two 32.768 kHz cycles after the event; once TIMEOUT has come the reset cannot be avoided. The watchdog is configured before START, after which CRV, RREN and CONFIG are locked until the device resets or wakes from System OFF.
Pins marked for standard drive and low-frequency use should carry only signals up to 10 kHz.

Reference circuits exist for the QIAA aQFN73, QFAA QFN48 and CKAA WLCSP; Nordic's PCB layouts and part values should be used for good RF performance. The circuits do not list every possible configuration, but between them they show all circuitry any configuration needs.

VDD can supply outside parts (the VEXT net) only while VDDH is powered. When the only source is USB, VBUS must be tied to VDDH for USB to work. The DC/DC parts are fitted only for a regulator stage whose DC/DC mode is enabled. NFC works in every configuration, and USB in every configuration as long as the host supplies VBUS. A series resistor, optional, in the USB supply line improves immunity to overvoltage transients when VBUS is plugged in, and is recommended for new designs. The aQFN73 RF match has two value sets, v1.0 and v1.1; the circuits use v1.1, which leaves more margin on spurious emissions in regulatory tests, though both are valid and all other RF figures are the same. The four-component aQFN73 match (configuration 7) suppresses harmonics better with TXPOWER at 5 dBm or above and is recommended for new designs; the three-component matches remain valid.

Follow the reference schematics and layouts closely, above all the matching parts between the ANT pin and the antenna: a layout change there can shift the match and cost RF performance. All reference circuits assume a 50 Ω single-ended antenna. Use at least two layers with a ground plane; with more layers, keep the inner layers clear under the matching network to cut stray capacitance. Decouple the supply right at the VDD pins with RF-grade capacitors, filter the chip's supply and route it apart from digital supplies, and avoid long supply traces. Keep all grounds, VDD connections and VDD bypass capacitors close to the IC. With a top-side ground plane tie the VSS pins straight to it; with a bottom ground plane put vias as close to the VSS pads as possible, at least one per VSS pin. Keep fast digital signals away from the crystal and the supply lines, keep the load on fast digital outputs small, and route the 32 MHz crystal lines away from the antenna line and its ground.

The example layout is for the aQFN73 with the internal LDO and VBUS supply. C3 is grounded through the VSS_PA pin (F23) rather than straight to the ground plane, which adds filtering of harmonics. No parts sit on the bottom layer.

The QFN48 package has no USB device (USBD), and its VDD and VDDH are shorted inside the package, so it works only in normal-voltage supply mode, never high-voltage mode. Its 1 Mbps Bluetooth LE sensitivity is -95 dBm typical and its maximum output power 7.5 dBm typical.

Every WLCSP variant reacts to visible and near infrared light, so the product must shield the chip by its enclosure or by shielding or coating the die. CKAA has a light-absorbing film on its marking side; its edges and ball side are still exposed and need protecting.
